verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow and out-of-bounds reads in NFC driver event handler. Attacker-controlled aid_len and params_len from packet data are used in memcpy without bounds checking against the allocated transaction struct size (skb->len - 2) or the skb data length. The initial validation uses && instead of ||, allowing short packets with a matching tag byte to bypass the check entirely.

evidence.reason: Logical error: uses && instead of ||. If skb->len is short (e.g., 1) but data[0]==0x81, the check passes and processing continues with insufficient data. Also reads skb->data[0] without checking skb->len >= 1.

evidence.snippet: transaction = devm_kzalloc(dev, skb->len - 2, GFP_KERNEL);
evidence.reason: Allocation size is based on raw skb->len - 2, not on the actual struct nfc_evt_transaction layout requirements. If skb->len < 2, unsigned underflow produces huge allocation. Does not account for struct field overhead (aid_len u32, aid[16], params_len u32).

aid_len (up to 255) is read from packet without validation against skb->len or NFC_MAX_AID_LENGTH(16). memcpy can overflow the aid[] field in the struct (heap overflow, CWE-122) and read OOB from skb (CWE-125).

evidence.snippet:
if (skb->data[transaction->aid_len + 2] !=
		    NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_PARAMS_TAG)
evidence.reason: Reads skb->data at offset aid_len + 2 without checking aid_len + 2 < skb->len. Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
params_len (up to 255) read from packet without validation. The memcpy can overflow the transaction allocation (heap overflow, CWE-122) and reads OOB from skb beyond skb->len (CWE-125).

assumptions: struct nfc_evt_transaction contains fixed-size fields: u32 aid_len, u8 aid[NFC_MAX_AID_LENGTH=16], u32 params_len, u8 params[] flexible array
skb->data contains attacker-controlled data from an NFC device (attacker can craft packets)
The event is received from an external NFC device which can be malicious
limitations: Exact struct definition not provided in the snippet; field sizes inferred from kernel NFC headers
The caller's behavior on skb ownership after return is not visible
Cannot confirm exact kernel version or whether additional validation exists upstream in nfc_hci layer

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability identified. All appended-trailer writes are bounded (tailroom check, ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE gate before page-frag use, skb_page_frag_refill size guarantee), shared page-frag state is protected by x->lock, page lifetime is pinned via get_page, and all error paths propagate correctly. The ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE guard that fixed the historical overlarge page-frag issue in this function is present.

evidence.reason: Bounds check before the page-frag path. It conservatively uses skb->data_len + tailen (u32 arithmetic with no realistic overflow given kernel skb size limits), and diverts oversized appends to the linearized skb_cow_data fallback, preventing oversized page-frag usage.

evidence.snippet: if (tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)) { nfrags = 1; trailer = skb; tail = skb_tail_pointer(trailer); goto skip_cow; }
evidence.reason: Linear-tail path writes only within verified tailroom; pskb_put extends the skb by exactly tailen bytes.

evidence.snippet: spin_lock_bh(&x->lock); if (unlikely(!skb_page_frag_refill(allocsize, pfrag, GFP_ATOMIC))) { ... goto cow; } page = pfrag->page; get_page(page); ... __skb_fill_page_desc(skb, nfrags, page, pfrag->offset, tailen); ... pfrag->offset = pfrag->offset + allocsize; spin_unlock_bh(&x->lock);
evidence.reason: Page-frag path: refill guarantee covers allocsize >= tailen bytes from pfrag->offset, so esp_output_fill_trailer's tfclen+2 bytes and the tailen-sized frag are in bounds. Shared per-SA pfrag state is mutated only under x->lock, and get_page pins the page against reuse/free. Failure falls back safely to cow.

COW path: skb_cow_data's return is error-checked; esph_offset is captured before reallocation and esp->esph is recomputed from the new transport header afterwards, avoiding stale-pointer use; nfrags is assigned on every path reaching the return.

assumptions: esp->tailen, esp->tfclen, esp->plen and esp->esph are set correctly by the callers (esp4/esp6 output paths), matching upstream kernel behavior.
ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE is the standard (PAGE_SIZE << SKB_FRAG_PAGE_ORDER)-style page-aligned constant larger than any possible tailen; its definition is not shown in the snippet.
skb->data_len is bounded well below UINT_MAX by kernel skb allocation/GSO limits, so the u32 addition skb->data_len + tailen cannot wrap.
limitations: Definitions and bodies of helpers (esp_output_encap, esp_output_fill_trailer, skb_page_frag_refill, skb_cow_data, pskb_put) and macro ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE are not provided; their correctness is assumed per upstream Linux semantics.
Callers of esp_output_head were not analyzed, so the origin and range of esp->tailen cannot be fully verified from the given code alone.
Analysis relies on the snippet matching the upstream fixed version of this function; if any referenced constant or helper deviates from upstream semantics, the conclusion could change.

verdict.summary: The function appears to be the patched (post-2.4.7) version of expat's addBinding. Reserved-prefix comparisons are bounds-safe via short-circuit NUL-terminated reads, the reserved URI check is bidirectional (mustBeXML != isXML), allocation sizes are guarded against int and size_t overflow (including the 32-bit multiplication case via the UINT_MAX >= SIZE_MAX guard), and the memcpy length is provably within the allocated buffer in all paths. No reachable memory-safety, bounds, or validation flaw is present in the given code.

assumptions: Callers always pass a non-NULL, NUL-terminated uri string (expat's storeAtts contract); otherwise the initial *uri dereference would be a NULL dereference, but upstream code shares this contract.
parser->m_dtd is non-NULL whenever addBinding is called, so the parser->m_dtd->defaultPrefix comparison at the end is safe.
b->uriAlloc and EXPAND_SPARE are such that len + EXPAND_SPARE is the allocated element count, matching the memcpy of len elements.
REALLOC/MALLOC are expat's allocator wrappers that set/propagate allocation failure as NULL.
limitations: Only this function was analyzed; vulnerabilities could exist in callers (e.g., how uri is produced or how bindings are freed via m_freeBindingList).
Configured compiler/platform variants (XML_Char width, size_t width) affect but do not break the overflow guards as written.

Prior known CVEs in this function (reserved-URI bypass, allocation overflow) are addressed by checks present in this code; however, absence of a NULL check on uri is noted as a defensive-coding gap that is only exploitable if a caller can pass NULL, which is not shown here.

verdict.summary: Index parameter 'u' is used to access fm->hdf[u] and fm->hd[u] without any bounds check against the number of stored headers, allowing an out-of-bounds read if a caller supplies an unvalidated index; fm->hd[u].b is also passed to strchr without a NULL check.

evidence.snippet: if (fm->hdf[u] & HDF_FILTER)
evidence.reason: Access to the hdf flags array with caller-supplied unsigned index 'u' and no prior bounds validation (no comparison against a header count such as fm->nhd). An out-of-range u yields an out-of-bounds read.

evidence.snippet: e = strchr(fm->hd[u].b, ':');
evidence.reason: Second unbounded array access fm->hd[u].b; additionally, .b is not checked for NULL before being passed to strchr, which would dereference NULL inside strchr if .b were NULL.

evidence.snippet: http_isfiltered(const struct http *fm, unsigned u, unsigned how)
evidence.reason: Function signature: 'u' is an unsigned index parameter with no documented or enforced upper bound; all safety depends on unseen callers, which is not guaranteed by the code itself.

assumptions: fm->hdf is a fixed-size flags array parallel to fm->hd, sized to a maximum header count, and a bound such as fm->nhd exists in struct http but is not checked here.
Callers may pass header indices derived from external/HTTP input in some paths; if all callers are provably in-range, severity drops.
The expression 'f != NULL && f->flag & how' was checked for precedence and parses as '(f != NULL) && (f->flag & how)', so there is no precedence or NULL-dereference bug there.
limitations: The full struct http definition, http_hdr_flags implementation, and all call sites are not provided, so out-of-bounds reachability and whether hd[u].b can be NULL cannot be definitively confirmed.

The original upstream implementation of this function typically includes an assert(u < http->nhd); its absence here is the basis for the finding, but build configuration (e.g., asserts enabled) is unknown.

verdict.summary: Unchecked calloc failure leaves mountent.mnt_opts NULL, which is then passed to addmntent, causing undefined behavior/NULL-pointer dereference in a privileged (setuid-root) mount helper. Secondary: mount_user and other mtab fields are written without sanitization, permitting potential mtab entry injection if unusual usernames are accepted.

evidence.reason: The result of calloc is only guarded for the option-building block; there is no error path when allocation fails, so execution continues with mnt_opts == NULL.

evidence.snippet: rc = addmntent(pmntfile, &mountent);
evidence.reason: addmntent is called unconditionally even when mountent.mnt_opts is NULL (calloc failure), leading to NULL-pointer dereference/undefined behavior in library string handling inside a privileged process.

mount_user (a username string) is embedded into the mtab options field without escaping commas, spaces, or newlines; a hostile username could inject or corrupt mtab entries. Typically mitigated by system username policy, hence lower confidence.

assumptions: addmntent treats mnt_opts as a NUL-terminated C string and does not accept NULL (typical libc behavior), so a NULL value results in undefined behavior, likely a crash.
getusername returns a NUL-terminated string or NULL; NULL is handled by the 'if (mount_user)' guard.
MOUNTED, EX_FILEIO, MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN, and the mtab lock helpers behave as in cifs-utils; unlock_mtab is safe to call twice (explicit call plus atexit handler).
This function runs in a setuid-root context (implied by setreuid(geteuid(), -1) rationale and toggle_dac_capability).
limitations: Only this function is provided; callee behavior (addmntent, getusername, my_endmntent, lock_mtab/unlock_mtab) is inferred, not verified.
The actual NULL-dereference occurs inside libc's addmntent; exact crash behavior is implementation-defined, so severity/confidence are moderated.
Caller-side validation of devname and mountpoint (which also flow into mtab) is unknown; mtab-injection risk via those fields cannot be assessed from this snippet.

verdict.summary: Unbounded signed-integer accumulation of the attacker-controlled octet counter (iOctetsRemain = iOctetsRemain*10 + c - '0') allows integer overflow to produce a negative count; error handling only logs and does not reset/reject the value, and the negative count then flows into an unclamped memcpy(dst, src, negative_count) in the OCTET_COUNTING branch, causing a remotely triggerable heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled size and content.

In the CP950 PUA handling path, the search loop over cp950_pua_tbl can exit with k equal to the table row count when the composed code c2 does not fall in any table range. The code then reads cp950_pua_tbl[k][0..3] without checking k against the table bounds, causing an out-of-bounds read of adjacent static memory whose contents can influence and be emitted in the converted output w.

evidence.reason: If no table row matches c2, the loop terminates with k == number of rows. The subsequent unconditional accesses cp950_pua_tbl[k][2], cp950_pua_tbl[k][0], etc., index one row past the end of the array (out-of-bounds read).

This guard admits a broad set of attacker-controlled (lead, trail) byte pairs from CP950 input; nothing guarantees c2 falls within any range listed in cp950_pua_tbl, so the non-matching (k == table size) case is reachable with crafted input.

The w computed from out-of-bounds table reads is emitted to the output function when positive, so OOB-read memory can influence/leak into converter output (info disclosure / undefined behavior); the w <= 0 fallback does not sanitize the garbage value.

assumptions: cp950_pua_tbl is a static 2D array of unsigned short with 4 columns (as implied by the sizeof computation), and big5_ucs_table/big5_ucs_table_size are consistent (the big5_ucs_table access is properly bounds-checked).
The input byte stream (lead byte via filter->cache, trail byte c) is attacker-controlled, as is typical for charset conversion of untrusted input.
This is the PHP mbstring (mbfl) Big5-to-UCS decoder; the missing post-loop bounds check on k is a known defect pattern in this function.
limitations: The declarations and actual contents of cp950_pua_tbl are not shown, so the exact number of rows and whether every admissible c2 is covered cannot be verified from the given code alone; the vulnerability depends on the existence of at least one admissible c2 not covered by any table range (structurally nothing prevents this).
Severity of the OOB read depends on memory layout beyond the table (adjacent static data); impact ranges from sanitizer abort/crash to minor information disclosure through the converted output.
No C standard library or unsafe pointer APIs are involved; the finding is limited to the array indexing issue.

verdict.summary: check_termcode() writes a NUL terminator at tp[len], i.e., buf[*buflen] or typebuf.tb_buf[tb_off+tb_len], which is one byte past the valid data region, without verifying *buflen < bufsize (or that the typebuf allocation has slack). If a caller passes a fully-filled buffer (*buflen == bufsize) or the typebuf is at its allocation edge, this is a 1-byte heap out-of-bounds write reachable while parsing attacker-controlled terminal input. Additionally, all forward-scanning reads (getdigits, get_bytes_from_buf/get_long_from_buf, and the KS_VER_SCROLLBAR/KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR loops, which advance j by +=3 with no length checks) rely solely on this sentinel for bounds, creating chained out-of-bounds-read risk if the invariant breaks. Minor: atoi() on attacker-supplied digit runs risks signed overflow (CWE-190).

evidence.snippet: tp[len] = NUL;
evidence.reason: Writes a NUL byte at tp[len], which equals buf[*buflen] (buf != NULL path) or typebuf.tb_buf[typebuf.tb_off + typebuf.tb_len] (buf == NULL path) — exactly one byte past the end of the valid data. The function never verifies *buflen < bufsize nor that the typebuf allocation extends beyond tb_off+tb_len; a caller passing a full buffer (*buflen == bufsize) causes a 1-byte heap out-of-bounds write while processing terminal input.

Bounds derivation for the buf path: offset + len == *buflen always, so the subsequent tp[len] = NUL writes at index *buflen, the first index past the data. Nothing constrains *buflen < bufsize here or at the write site.

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; tp[j] == CSI && tp[j + 1] == KS_VER_SCROLLBAR && tp[j + 2] != NUL; ++i) { j += 3; num_bytes = get_bytes_from_buf(tp + j, bytes, 1); ... }
evidence.reason: The scrollbar loops advance j by 3 and by num_bytes without any comparison against len; get_bytes_from_buf()/get_long_from_buf() scan forward until a NUL byte with no length parameter. Their safety depends entirely on the tp[len] = NUL sentinel being present and in bounds; if the sentinel write is out of the reachable region or the buffer is resized (handle_csi/put_string_in_typebuf receive bufsize/buflen and may alter them), these become out-of-bounds reads.

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; tp[j] == CSI && tp[j + 1] == KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR && tp[j + 2] != NUL; ++i) { j += 3; num_bytes = get_long_from_buf(tp + j, &val); ... }
evidence.reason: Same pattern as the vertical scrollbar loop: unbounded relative reads (up to 4 bytes per get_long_from_buf) guarded only by NUL short-circuiting against the sentinel byte, which itself may be written out of bounds.

evidence.snippet: modifiers_start = tp + slen - 2; n = atoi((char *)modifiers_start); modifiers |= decode_modifiers(n);
evidence.reason: atoi() is applied to an attacker-controlled digit sequence from terminal input (bounded only by the sentinel); a sufficiently long digit run overflows int (undefined behavior, CWE-190), though decode_modifiers likely masks the result (not shown).

assumptions: Line numbers are approximate; the code was provided without line annotations.
char_u is an unsigned char typedef; CSI/ESC/DCS/OSC are single-byte control values as in Vim.
get_bytes_from_buf/get_long_from_buf scan forward until a NUL byte and do not receive a length parameter, matching historical Vim implementations.

The severity of the tp[len] = NUL write depends on caller invariants (e.g., callers passing *buflen < bufsize and the typebuf allocation including slack) that are not visible in this code; upstream Vim mitigates this with extra allocation bytes for exactly this reason.
limitations: Callers of check_termcode() and the allocation sizes of buf and typebuf.tb_buf are not shown, so it cannot be conclusively proven that *buflen == bufsize is reachable.

Implementations of getdigits, get_bytes_from_buf, get_long_from_buf, handle_csi, handle_osc, handle_dcs, put_string_in_typebuf, modifiers2keycode, and decode_modifiers are not shown; their internal bounds checks were assumed per historical Vim behavior.
GUI-only paths (scrollbar, menu pointer cast) are unlikely to be directly attacker-controllable from a terminal in a GUI session, reducing practical exploitability of those specific branches.
Preprocessor configuration (FEAT_GUI, FEAT_MOUSE_*, USE_ON_FLY_SCROLL, FEAT_TERMRESPONSE) affects which paths compile; analysis covers all shown variants.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability demonstrable from the given code. All client-controlled lengths (optlen, exportnamelen, nrinfos, nr_queries, querylen) are bounds-checked before any memory access: optlen is capped at MAX_REQUEST_SIZE before allocation, optlen-6 and optlen-8 subtractions are guarded by preceding optlen>=6 / optlen>=8 checks, the NBD_OPT_INFO/GO path validates exportnamelen before reading nrinfos and enforces the exact structural length optlen == 4+exportnamelen+2+2*nrinfos before the info loop, and the meta-context loop maintains opt_index <= optlen across all iterations. TLS=require enforcement is correct, STARTTLS replay is blocked and cached state is reset after upgrade, and option-count/size limits mitigate DoS. Safety of the meta-context path depends on check_export_name/check_string enforcing their maxlen parameters, which the call-site usage pattern strongly indicates they do.

evidence.reason: optlen is validated against MAX_REQUEST_SIZE before allocation and before any conn_recv_full into data, preventing oversized reads; optlen+1 cannot wrap provided MAX_REQUEST_SIZE < UINT32_MAX (a named protocol limit).

The optlen>=6 check prevents underflow of optlen-6, and the explicit exportnamelen bound check guarantees the 2-byte read at data[exportnamelen+4] stays within [0, optlen); the later structural equality check (optlen == 4+exportnamelen+2+2*nrinfos) bounds the info-request loop reads exactly to optlen.

optlen>=8 prevents underflow of optlen-8; exportnamelen (client-controlled 32-bit) is validated via check_export_name with maxlen=optlen-8 before use in strndup/opt_index, and each subsequent 4-byte header read is guarded by opt_index+4 > optlen with opt_index bounded by optlen (no uint32 overflow reachable given MAX_REQUEST_SIZE).

Loop invariant opt_index <= optlen is maintained: each querylen is bounded by check_string against optlen - opt_index (non-negative under the invariant), so opt_index += querylen never exceeds optlen and strncmp/memcpy reads remain in bounds.

evidence.snippet:
if (tls == 2 && !conn->using_tls &&
    !(option == NBD_OPT_ABORT || option == NBD_OPT_STARTTLS)) { ... continue; }
evidence.reason: FORCEDTLS mode correctly restricts pre-TLS options to ABORT/STARTTLS, blocks TLS double-negotiation via conn->using_tls, wipes cached state (structured_replies, default_exportname) after upgrade, and enforces TLS at the end of negotiation; no downgrade/bypass path found.

assumptions: MAX_REQUEST_SIZE is a small compile-time protocol limit (< UINT32_MAX and < INT_MAX), so optlen+1 cannot wrap and the (int)querylen cast in the debug call is safe.

check_export_name(option, str, len, maxlen) and check_string(...) return -1 when len > maxlen, i.e., they enforce their maxlen parameter; the code's consistent (len, maxlen) call pattern and the fact that NBD_OPT_LIST/SET_META_CONTEXT relies on check_export_name's failure to reject oversized exportnamelen strongly implies this. The safety of the strndup(&data[4], exportnamelen) call depends on this.

finish_newstyle_options validates/uses the export name with its length parameter and, per the in-code comment, drops the previously set meta context when the NBD_OPT_GO export name differs from the one used in NBD_OPT_SET_META_CONTEXT.
send_newstyle_option_reply_info_str treats a length of -1 (SIZE_MAX when passed via size_t, or -1 after conversion) as 'use strlen(name)', matching the namelen = -1 usage for the default export name.
conn_recv_full reads exactly the requested number of bytes and fails otherwise.
limitations: Helper functions (check_export_name, check_string, finish_newstyle_options, conn_recv_full, send_newstyle_option_reply_*) are not shown; the verdict relies on their enforcing the bounds suggested by their signatures and usage.

The buffer data is allocated with malloc(optlen + 1) and the trailing byte data[optlen] is never initialized; if any not-shown helper treated data as a NUL-terminated string rather than using explicit lengths, that would be an uninitialized-read issue, but no such use is visible in the given code.

Minor non-security robustness issues: debug printf uses %d with uint32_t values (nr_queries) and (int)querylen, which could print negative values for pathological lengths, but do not affect memory safety.
The values of constants such as MAX_NR_OPTIONS, MAX_REQUEST_SIZE, NBD option codes, and the tls mode variable are not shown and were assumed to take their conventional nbdkit values.

verdict.summary: win_redr_status appends the ' ' separator and status flags ([Help], [Preview], [+], [RO]) to the fixed-size NameBuff buffer without checking that len < MAXPATHL - 1. A buffer name that fills NameBuff completely (len == MAXPATHL - 1) causes the space write to destroy the NUL terminator; the subsequent STRLEN(p + len) reads out of bounds, and any resulting len > MAXPATHL makes 'MAXPATHL - len' negative, which is converted to a huge size_t in vim_snprintf, enabling an out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: No bounds check before *(p + len++) = ' '. If the buffer name (from get_trans_bufname into NameBuff, max MAXPATHL-1 chars) has len == MAXPATHL-1, the space write replaces the NUL terminator at the last valid index and len becomes MAXPATHL. The following vim_snprintf(p + MAXPATHL, 0, ...) writes nothing, but len += STRLEN(p + len) reads from one past the end of NameBuff (unterminated string) — an out-of-bounds read that leaves len attacker-influenced and possibly > MAXPATHL.

If len has been corrupted past MAXPATHL by the preceding out-of-bounds STRLEN, the int expression MAXPATHL - len is negative and is implicitly converted to size_t (variadic call to vim_snprintf), yielding an enormous length limit; the write destination p + len is already outside NameBuff, enabling an out-of-bounds write beyond the fixed-size buffer.

NameBuff is a fixed-size buffer (MAXPATHL bytes) populated with the (attacker-influenceable) buffer name. len can legitimately equal MAXPATHL - 1 (a maximally long path/buffer name), which is the precondition that makes the unguarded appends below unsafe. No truncation or bounds validation is performed between this point and the flag-appending writes.

assumptions: NameBuff is a global fixed-size char_u array of MAXPATHL (1024) bytes, as in Vim's standard globals.
vim_snprintf's size parameter is size_t; a negative int argument is implicitly converted to a very large value.
vim_snprintf performs no writes when the size argument is 0, so the immediate failure mode at len == MAXPATHL is the out-of-bounds STRLEN read, which then corrupts len.
The buffer name can reach length MAXPATHL - 1 (e.g., a very long file path or buffer name set by a plugin/modeline/attacker-controlled context).
limitations: Definitions of get_trans_bufname, vim_snprintf, NameBuff, mb_string2cells, and the screen_* functions are not included, so their exact bounds behavior is assumed from typical Vim implementations.
Exploitability of the out-of-bounds write depends on the value read by the out-of-bounds STRLEN (adjacent global/heap data), so the write primitive is probabilistic rather than deterministic.

The multibyte truncation branch and the this_ru_col clamping appear internally consistent; no distinct vulnerability was identified there beyond propagation of a corrupted len into screen_fill's start column.

verdict.summary: Reachable undefined behavior (shift by 32, i.e., by the full width of unsigned int) in the bitfield mask decoding loops of ReadBMPImage. An attacker-controlled BI_BITFIELDS mask with bit 31 and bit 0 set (e.g., 0x80000001) drives the 'sample' loops so that 'mask << sample' is evaluated with sample == 32 before the '> 32U' guard breaks the loop. The UB result feeds ClampToQuantum and pixel reconstruction for 16/32-bpp images, producing platform-dependent, potentially compiler-optimized-away behavior. The rest of the coder is otherwise bounds-checked (colormap counts, ReadBlob counts, seek results, IsValidColormapIndex, per-case stride recomputations).

evidence.reason: The break guard 'sample > 32U' is evaluated only after sample has been incremented to 32 and only after the loop condition has already evaluated 'bmp_info.red_mask << 32'. With an attacker-supplied mask having bit 31 and bit 0 set (BI_BITFIELDS, bits_per_pixel 16 or 32), the condition remains true through sample=31, so the loop performs a shift whose count equals the width of unsigned int (32) before breaking at 33 — undefined behavior (CWE-758). The identical pattern is repeated for green_mask, blue_mask, and alpha_mask.

Related shift loop sharing the same '> 32U' guard idiom. For this first family the exit at shift <= 31 is guaranteed for any nonzero mask, so no UB occurs here, but it confirms the off-by-one guard style ('> 32' instead of '>= 32') that produces the UB in the sample loops.

assumptions: DecodeImage, IsValidColormapIndex, ReadBlob/ReadBlobLSBLong, SeekBlob, AcquireVirtualMemory, and SetImageExtent behave as in ImageMagick/MagickCore: DecodeImage respects the passed buffer length, IsValidColormapIndex rejects out-of-range indices, AcquireVirtualMemory checks for size overflow, and SetImageExtent enforces width/height resource limits.
size_t is 64-bit, so products like image->columns*bmp_info.bits_per_pixel and bytes_per_line*image->rows do not wrap for the bounded dimension values that survive SetImageExtent.

Per-case recomputed strides (2*(columns+columns%2) for 16bpp, 4*((columns*24+31)/32) for 24bpp, 4*columns for 32bpp) were verified to be no larger than the originally allocated row stride for all column parities, so no heap over-read arises from them.
limitations: Line numbers are unavailable because the source was provided without a file context.
The external helper DecodeImage (RLE decoding) is not shown; RLE-specific memory-safety bugs cannot be assessed from the given code.

The shift-by-32 UB was judged low severity: on mainstream hardware it yields incorrect/platform-dependent pixel values rather than memory corruption, though standards-conforming compilers may exploit the UB.

Secondary robustness weaknesses were observed but not scored as vulnerabilities: bmp_info is not re-initialized between frames of a multi-frame file (stale start_position/alpha_mask across BA-frames), header field reads are not checked for EOF (later sanity checks usually convert truncation into exceptions), and the file_size mismatch produces only a warning in one branch.

verdict.summary: FindEmptyObjectSlot performs a correctly bounded scan (i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS) over s_objects, NULL-checks the optional handle out-parameter before writing, uses non-overflowing handle arithmetic (small loop bound added to a fixed base), and defensively zeroes the entire OBJECT before reuse, preventing residual-data leakage. No memory-safety, bounds, integer, or lifetime issues are present in this code.

evidence.reason: Loop is bounded by MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS so &s_objects[i] stays in bounds; handle is NULL-checked before dereference; i + TRANSIENT_FIRST cannot overflow a UINT32 given the small loop bound; MemorySet(object, 0, sizeof(*object)) zeroes exactly the whole struct (wiping residual sensitive data, including attributes) before reuse; NULL is returned on exhaustion, leaving the safety of that path to the caller.

assumptions: s_objects is an array of at least MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS OBJECT elements, as in the standard TPM2/libtpms implementation.
TRANSIENT_FIRST and MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS are compile-time constants small enough that i + TRANSIENT_FIRST cannot wrap UINT32 and remains within the valid transient handle range.
MemorySet(ptr, val, size) has memset-like semantics.
This function is called in a single-threaded TPM execution context, so no concurrency/TOCTOU window exists here.
limitations: Caller-side handling of the NULL return is not shown; a missing NULL check by callers would be a separate vulnerability in the calling code, not in this function.
Declarations/definitions of s_objects, MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS, TRANSIENT_FIRST, OBJECT, and MemorySet are not included, so array sizing and constant values are assumed per the standard implementation.
Concurrency model of the surrounding system is not visible from this snippet.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read of 2 bytes at buffer offset 6 for number_of_classes without verifying sz >= 8; additionally, a possibly-NULL constant-pool object is passed to further calls unchecked, the fallback path frees an entry whose name was successfully allocated (leaking name and flags_str), and the classes list allocation is not NULL-checked.

evidence.snippet:

verdict.summary: kvmppc_rtas_hcall computes args.rets = &args.args[be32_to_cpu(args.nargs)] using a fully guest-controlled, unvalidated nargs (and never validates nret). Because rtas_args.args holds only 16 words, a guest can set nargs so that args.rets points out of bounds of the kernel-stack struct; the dispatched RTAS handler (d->handler->handler) then writes return values through args.rets, producing a kernel stack out-of-bounds write with a guest-chosen offset — a guest-to-host privilege-escape primitive.

There is no bounds check against ARRAY_SIZE(args.args) (16 entries) before it is used as an array index to form a write pointer. This is an unvalidated guest-controlled index (CWE-129) that yields a pointer potentially gigabytes past the stack object (CWE-787/CWE-121).

If the guest supplies a valid token, the RTAS handler is invoked with &args; per the RTAS ABI handlers store return values through args.rets (i.e., args.args[nargs + i]). Since nargs is unbounded, these stores land out of bounds of the 16-word args array on the kernel stack, corrupting adjacent stack data (including saved registers / return address) with guest-influenced 32-bit values.

The entire struct rtas_args — including nargs, nret, and the args array — is copied unvalidated from guest memory. The only check performed is on the return code of the read; no field of args is ever validated anywhere in the function (no check on nargs or nargs+nret against the array size), which is the root enabling condition for the OOB write.

assumptions: struct rtas_args matches the PowerPC KVM definition: __be32 token; __be32 nargs; __be32 nret; __be32 args[16]; __be32 *rets — so args has a fixed capacity of 16 argument words.

Registered RTAS handlers (e.g., RTAS read/write PCI config, logical CI access) write their return values via args.rets per the RTAS firmware ABI, and the guest can register/map at least one token in practice.
The guest is untrusted or compromised; KVM guests issue this hcall directly, so this is a guest-to-host kernel attack surface.
sizeof(args) is a compile-time constant, so the kvm_read_guest/kvm_write_guest copies themselves are size-safe; the vulnerability lies exclusively in the unchecked index used to form args.rets.
limitations: The snippet does not include the handler implementations, so the exact values written through the OOB rets pointer (and hence the exploitability ceiling beyond 'semi-controlled 32-bit writes') cannot be fully characterized from this code alone.
The upstream fix (adding nargs / nargs+nret bounds checks before the args.rets fixup) is not present here; analysis is based solely on the code as given.
Line numbers in evidence are estimated from the function body as presented, not from an authoritative source file.

verdict.summary: On KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND the function sets rc=1, reporting the keytab as available when the requested key was not found. This inverted logic can mislead callers and enable authentication bypass or unintended Kerberos operation without a valid key.

evidence.reason: When krb5_kt_get_entry returns KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND, the key does not exist in the keytab, yet rc is set to 1 (available). Correct behavior would be rc=0, making this an inverted logic flaw that causes a missing key to be reported as present.

assumptions: rc=1 means 'available' to callers, consistent with the success path returning 1.
Callers use this function to gate Kerberos-based authentication (kssl context).
limitations: Actual exploitability depends on how callers of this function handle a 'true' return value.
No memory-safety, bounds, or input-validation issues were found in this function in isolation.
entry is uninitialized at declaration but not dereferenced before assignment by krb5_kt_get_entry.

verdict.summary: ax25_release() calls ax25_disconnect() after releasing the socket lock; ax25_disconnect() may internally call ax25_destroy_socket() and free the ax25_cb (when SOCK_DESTROY is set) or a concurrent timer/softirq may free it during the unlocked window. The caller then dereferences ax25 (sock_flag(ax25->sk, SOCK_DESTROY)) or calls ax25_destroy_socket(ax25) again, producing use-after-free / double-free. Additionally, the AX25_STATE_3/4 path dereferences ax25->ax25_dev->values[...] without a NULL check even though the same pointer is NULL-checked later in the function.

evidence.reason: In AX25_STATE_0, the lock is dropped before ax25_disconnect(). ax25_disconnect() invokes ax25_destroy_socket() and frees the ax25_cb when the socket has SOCK_DESTROY set (or via concurrent timer callbacks during the unlocked window). The subsequent unconditional ax25_destroy_socket(ax25) then operates on freed memory: use-after-free / double-free of the ax25_cb.

Same unlocked-window pattern in AX25_STATE_1/2. If ax25_disconnect() frees ax25 internally (SOCK_DESTROY set on sk), the sock_flag(ax25->sk, ...) read dereferences the freed ax25_cb. The unlocked interval between release_sock and lock_sock also allows a concurrent path or timer to free ax25 before it is used again.

evidence.snippet: switch (ax25->ax25_dev->values[AX25_VALUES_PROTOCOL]) {
evidence.reason: ax25->ax25_dev is dereferenced without any NULL check, while the function itself later guards the identical pointer with 'if (ax25_dev)' (line 76), demonstrating that ax25->ax25_dev can be NULL for a socket reaching this code. If state 3/4 is reached without a bound device, this is a NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476).

The T1 timer is restarted with a raw ax25 pointer and destruction is deferred to timer-driven paths while SOCK_DESTROY is set; combined with the unlocked ax25_disconnect() calls elsewhere in the function, this creates a lifetime window in which the timer callback can free ax25 concurrently (CWE-367 race / UAF), consistent with known ax25 timer use-after-free bugs.

assumptions: ax25_disconnect(), ax25_destroy_socket(), and timer callbacks are taken from the upstream Linux AX.25 implementation, where ax25_destroy_socket() kfree()s the ax25_cb and ax25_disconnect() calls ax25_destroy_socket() when SOCK_DESTROY is set on the socket.
sk lifetime is protected by the explicit sock_hold()/sock_put() pair; the vulnerability concerns the ax25_cb, which is freed by callees without the caller's knowledge.
limitations: The definitions of ax25_disconnect, ax25_destroy_socket, and the timer functions are not included in the snippet; the free-inside-callee behavior is inferred from the upstream implementation this code matches.
Exploitability (attacker-controlled timing of the concurrent free vs. reachability of NULL ax25_dev in state 3/4) depends on call sites not shown here.

verdict.summary: The function maintains a verified invariant (allocated usable size >= offsetof(actions) + actions_len) across all paths: the fast path validates space with non-underflowing size_t arithmetic, the growth path clamps to MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE only after an explicit fail-closed re-check, the reallocation always allocates at least next_offset + req_size bytes, the state (actions_len, orig_len) is copied correctly field-to-field, and the old buffer is freed exactly once before the pointer is updated. The out-path increments actions_len only after space is proven. No reachable memory-safety, lifetime, or integer-overflow flaw exists in this function; remaining concerns (uninitialized padding bytes and int/size_t mixing) depend on caller behavior not shown.

evidence.snippet:
if (req_size <= (ksize(*sfa) - next_offset))
		goto out;
evidence.reason: Fast-path bounds check. Because next_offset <= ksize(*sfa) is an invariant (established and preserved on every path), the size_t subtraction never underflows; a wrapped 'huge' available-space value (classic bypass pattern) cannot occur here.

Cap enforcement is fail-closed: if next_offset ever reached/exceeded MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE, the int subtraction would be negative, which is strictly less than the positive req_size, producing an -EMSGSIZE error rather than allowing an undersized allocation. When clamped, MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE >= next_offset + req_size is guaranteed by this same check.

Reallocation allocates at least next_offset + req_size bytes (per the max() and cap logic), copies only actions_len bytes from the old buffer (within its actual ksize), preserves state fields correctly without swapping actions_len/orig_len, and frees the old buffer exactly once with no subsequent dereference — no UAF, double-free, or out-of-bounds copy.

actions_len is only incremented after available space was proven (fast-path check) or a sufficiently large reallocation succeeded; the returned pointer therefore always has at least req_size writable bytes, preserving the invariant across repeated calls.

assumptions: Callers pass attr_len derived from netlink attribute lengths (nla_len / nla_total_size), i.e., small non-negative values (u16-bounded), so the theoretical NLA_ALIGN(int) overflow for negative or near-INT_MAX attr_len is not reachable.
nla_alloc_flow_actions returns an allocation whose usable size (ksize) is >= the requested new_acts_size, which is the standard kmalloc guarantee.
The caller (e.g., ovs_nla_add_action) initializes the returned region including nla padding, as done in the upstream module; the reserved bytes are not zeroed by this function itself.
MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE (32 KiB) fits comfortably in int, and ksize of the flow-actions buffer is far below values that would overflow the int/size_t mixing at the new_acts_size assignment.
limitations: Only this single function was analyzed; caller-side behavior (validation of attr_len, initialization of padding bytes before netlink dump) is out of scope and would determine whether an info leak via uninitialized padding bytes is possible.

This code matches the hardened upstream Linux implementation (including the MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE cap and orig_len handling); if embedded in a codebase where attr_len can be attacker-controlled 32-bit value (not u16-bounded), the int overflow at NLA_ALIGN(attr_len) and the truncating assignment to int new_acts_size would become real hazards (CWE-190).

verdict.summary: In VREPLACE mode, change_indent() writes new_line[curwin->w_cursor.col] = NUL into a vim_strsave()-allocated buffer sized strlen(line)+1, without validating that w_cursor.col is within the line length. w_cursor.col is derived from the caller's unvalidated cursor column offset (new_cursor_col = original col - first-non-blank col, plus the post-indent first-non-blank column) and is only lower-clamped at 0, so a cursor column exceeding the resulting line length (e.g., after indent shrinkage or when the cursor was positioned past end-of-line) causes an out-of-bounds heap write. The corrupted buffer is subsequently passed to ins_bytes(), propagating heap corruption. The same unvalidated column can also drive an unbounded replace-push loop in REPLACE mode.

evidence.reason: vim_strsave() allocates exactly strlen(line)+1 bytes, but w_cursor.col is used as an index with no bound check. Since w_cursor.col is not validated against the line length anywhere in the function (only clamped to >= 0), a cursor column larger than the current line length results in a heap buffer out-of-bounds write.

The final cursor column is set from new_cursor_col, which in the new_cursor_col >= 0 branch is a raw arithmetic offset (original cursor column minus first-non-blank column, plus the new first-non-blank column after set_indent/shift_line). It is only lower-clamped at 0 and never compared to the current line length, allowing w_cursor.col to exceed the length of the (possibly shortened) line.

In this branch, new_cursor_col is an unvalidated byte offset from the first non-blank, derived from the caller's cursor column. Unlike the insert-mode branch, there is no bounded walk of the actual line to compute it, so the resulting column is not guaranteed to lie within the line after set_indent() or shift_line() has altered its length.
If w_cursor.col is inflated beyond the line length (same root cause), this loop performs an unbounded number of replace_push() calls, enabling unbounded memory growth on the replace stack.

assumptions: Vim context is assumed: vim_strsave allocates strlen(line)+1 bytes including the NUL terminator; w_cursor.col is a colnr_T column index into the current line.
set_indent()/shift_line() may shorten the line (e.g., INDENT_DEC or a smaller indent) and reposition the cursor on the first non-blank.
The caller can supply a cursor column that is at or past the end of the current line (possible in virtual replace mode and related cursor states), which is the trigger for the out-of-bounds write.
Exact line numbers are approximate because the snippet is a function body without file context.
limitations: The vulnerability trigger depends on runtime state (cursor position relative to line length, VREPLACE mode) not fully determinable from the function body alone; the proof requires a call path where w_cursor.col exceeds the post-change line length.
Helper functions (set_indent, shift_line, ins_str, ml_replace, backspace_until_column, replace_push) are not shown, so their exact cursor/length semantics are inferred from Vim conventions.

No proof of exploitability (controlled data past the allocation) is established from this code alone; the finding is an out-of-bounds write of a single NUL byte beyond a heap buffer, followed by use of the corrupted buffer in ins_bytes().

verdict.summary: apprentice_load() leaks the filearr array and all duplicated filename strings when an error path (snprintf failure or erealloc failure) triggers 'goto out' from inside the directory-reading loop, since the out: block never frees filearr (CWE-401, enabling memory-exhaustion DoS via repeated invocations). It also follows symlinks via stat() rather than lstat() and has a TOCTOU window between the stat() type check and load_1()'s later open, allowing an attacker with directory write access to substitute which file gets loaded (CWE-367/CWE-59). Additionally, overlong constructed paths are silently truncated to MAXPATHLEN-1 and the truncated (incorrect) filename is used for loading magic definitions (CWE-170). No memory-safety overflow was found in the estrndup length clamping or the maxfiles growth arithmetic.

evidence.reason: Error path jumps to 'out:' without freeing filearr or the filearr[0..files-1] strings already allocated in prior iterations; the out: block only frees mset entries and map->magic arrays. Same leak applies to the erealloc failure path. Repeated triggering (directory with entries plus forced allocation failure conditions) leads to unbounded memory growth.

stat() follows symlinks, so a symlink to any regular file passes the S_ISREG check; combined with the gap between this stat() and load_1()'s open of the same path, an attacker able to modify the directory contents can race the check (TOCTOU, CWE-367) or redirect loading to an arbitrary file (CWE-59).

evidence.snippet: filearr[files++] = estrndup(mfn, (mflen > sizeof(mfn) - 1)? sizeof(mfn) - 1: mflen);
evidence.reason: When snprintf truncates (mflen >= sizeof(mfn)), the code silently clamps the length instead of rejecting the entry; the resulting duplicated string is a truncated, incorrect path that is subsequently passed to load_1() and loaded as a magic file, an unvalidated-path construction flaw (CWE-170). The clamp itself does stay within the mfn buffer (snprintf NUL-terminates at MAXPATHLEN-1 valid chars), so there is no out-of-bounds read here.

Unchecked size_t multiplication maxfiles * sizeof(*filearr) could theoretically overflow (CWE-190), though reaching it requires an implausible number of directory entries; also, on NULL return the previous filearr pointer is lost (leak). In PHP's allocator, erealloc failure is normally fatal, making the NULL branch dead code.

assumptions: Line numbers are approximated by counting from the first line of the provided snippet since no original file/line metadata was given.
MAXPATHLEN is the size of mfn and of d.d_name in php_stream_dirent; php_stream_readdir NUL-terminates d.d_name.
erealloc/estrndup/efree are PHP's emalloc-family allocators; erealloc typically terminates the process on allocation failure rather than returning NULL.
load_1, set_text_binary, coalesce_entries, cmpstrp, and magic_entry_free are external and assumed to manage their own memory/bounds correctly.
limitations: Loop termination of the inner 'for (i = 0; i < mset[j].count; )' loop depends on set_text_binary()'s return value; a non-advancing return when cont_level == 0 would cause an infinite loop, but this cannot be confirmed from the given code.
The practical exploitability of the TOCTOU requires an attacker with write access to the magic-files directory; the code does not indicate what privilege context fn is under.
The maxfiles overflow (CWE-190) is only a theoretical concern and was not counted toward the verdict.
The noted FIXME about non-deterministic file ordering (missing sort before load, Debian bug #488562) affects behavior stability but is not a direct memory-safety vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The return value of krb5_sname_to_principal is never checked, so on failure a NULL principal is passed to krb5_kt_get_entry, risking a NULL dereference/crash (DoS). Additionally, KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND is mapped to rc=1 ('keytab available'), causing the function to report success even when the required service key is missing, misleading callers that decide whether to enable Kerberos authentication.

evidence.snippet:
krb5rc = krb5_sname_to_principal(krb5context, NULL, 
                                     kssl_ctx->service_name ? kssl_ctx->service_name: KRB5SVC,
                                     KRB5_NT_SRV_HST, &princ);

    krb5rc = krb5_kt_get_entry(krb5context, krb5keytab, 
                                princ,
                                0 /* IGNORE_VNO */,
                                0 /* IGNORE_ENCTYPE */,
                                &entry);
evidence.reason: The return code of krb5_sname_to_principal is assigned but never checked and is immediately overwritten. If the call fails, princ stays NULL and is then passed to krb5_kt_get_entry, which is undefined behavior and a potential NULL-pointer dereference inside the krb5 library, crashing the server process (denial of service).

When the required service key entry is not found in the keytab, the function sets rc = 1, reporting the keytab as 'available'. This inverts the expected failure semantics: callers will conclude a usable service principal key exists and may enable Kerberos authentication processing when it does not.

assumptions: The krb5 library's krb5_kt_get_entry does not tolerate a NULL principal (typical behavior is a crash or undefined behavior); if it explicitly NULL-checks, the crash risk is reduced.
Callers use the return value (1 = available) to decide whether to proceed with Kerberos/SSL-GSSAPI handling, as in OpenSSL's kssl usage.
kssl_ctx is a valid, non-NULL context provided by the caller; its validation is out of scope of the shown code.
limitations: Only this single function is shown; the actual exploitability depends on caller behavior and on whether kssl_ctx->service_name or environment can be influenced by an attacker.

The KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND -> rc=1 mapping may be a deliberate (if debatable) design choice in the original OpenSSL kssl.c, where 'keytab available' means the keytab file itself was readable; impact therefore depends on the caller's contract.
Severity of the NULL-principal issue depends on the linked krb5 implementation version, which is not provided.

verdict.summary: The LZW decoder's output loop writes to the context stack via repeated *stack_pos++ with no bounds check against the end of the stack buffer, relying entirely on external sizing invariants. More critically, the 'code not in table' (KwKwK) branch uses ctx->previous_code and ctx->previous_code_first without validating they were initialized; on the first decoded code (or first code after a clear), code_new can equal current_entry, making code_out an uninitialized value that is used as a table index in the while loop, enabling an out-of-bounds read of the dictionary and potentially unbounded writes to the output stack.

evidence.reason: KwKwK path dereferences ctx->previous_code and ctx->previous_code_first without any check that they have been initialized. On the first code after init/clear, code_new can equal current_entry (e.g., clear_code=4 gives current_entry=6 while a first 4-bit code can be 6), so this branch is reachable with uninitialized state.

No bounds check on stack_pos against the end of the buffer at ctx->stack_base; if code_out is uninitialized/stale (from the KwKwK path), table + code_out is an out-of-bounds read and the loop can emit an unbounded number of bytes past the stack buffer.
Code validation is present but performed against current_entry and the code-size cap; it does not validate ctx->previous_code, which is the value actually used as the chain start in the KwKwK branch.

assumptions: table has (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) entries and stack_base points to a fixed-size buffer whose size cannot be verified from this code
lzw__next_code reads exactly current_code_size bits, so code_new <= (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) - 1
lzw_init and lzw__clear_codes are not shown; whether they initialize previous_code/previous_code_first and reset the table is unknown

If the caller guarantees streams begin with a Clear code AND clear/init sanitize previous_code, and the stack buffer is sized >= table size, the in-bounds/termination invariants hold and this code would be memory-safe
limitations: Only lzw_decode is provided; the lzw_ctx layout, stack buffer size, lzw_init, lzw__clear_codes, and lzw__next_code implementations are not visible

The chain-length invariant (previous_entry strictly less than entry index, max emission ~ (1<<LZW_CODE_MAX) - clear_code) suggests safety under correct buffer sizing, so exploitability hinges on the unseen initialization and buffer sizing code, hence reduced confidence

verdict.summary: rpa_read_buffer uses `if (p > end)` before dereferencing `*p++`. When the cursor equals `end` (no bytes remaining), the length byte is read one byte past the end of the buffer, causing a one-byte out-of-bounds read (potential crash/DoS or minor info leak). The bounds check for the memcpy body is otherwise sound since len is a single byte (max 255), preventing pointer-overflow bypasses.

evidence.reason: The guard rejects only p > end, so p == end passes. `len = *p++` then dereferences the pointer at `end`, reading one byte past the end of the input buffer (out-of-bounds read, CWE-125). A check such as `p >= end` (or verifying at least one byte remains) is missing before the dereference.

The body bounds check and memcpy are safe: len is derived from a single byte (max 255), so p + len cannot overflow the pointer arithmetic and wrap around the comparison. This confirms the only memory-safety issue is the earlier length-byte dereference.

assumptions: `end` points one past the last valid byte of the input buffer (exclusive end, standard C convention).
`*data` initially points within or at the end of the buffer; `p` and `end` point into the same allocation.
`p_malloc` aborts on allocation failure (Dovecot-style pool allocator), so a NULL return need not be handled.
limitations: If `end` were inclusive (pointing at the last valid byte), the `p > end` check would be correct and no OOB read would occur; the conclusion depends on the exclusive-end convention, which is not shown in the given code.
Actual exploitability (crash vs. silent OOB byte) depends on the caller's buffer layout and how callers drive `*data` toward `end`, which is outside the provided code.
len == 0 returns success with a zero-length buffer, making the return value 0 ambiguous with the error path — a minor API robustness issue, not a memory-safety vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The function is the hardened libtiff implementation: attacker-influenced tdir_count is clamped by maxcount and two explicit 2GB sanity checks prevent uint32/tmsize_t overflow; typesize==0 is rejected before division; allocation size provably equals the subsequent memcpy/file-read length (datasize <= 2147483647); small-value copies (<=4 or <=8 bytes) read within the 8-byte tdir_offset union; errors free the buffer. The only theoretical defect, division by zero if a caller passed desttypesize==0, is not attacker-reachable since callers pass compile-time sizeof constants.

evidence.reason: typesize==0 (attacker-controlled via tdir_type) is rejected before the 2147483647/typesize division, preventing div-by-zero; the sanity check bounds target_count64 so the later (uint32) cast and datasize computation cannot overflow.

evidence.snippet:
if ((uint64)(2147483647/desttypesize)<target_count64)
    return(TIFFReadDirEntryErrSizesan);
evidence.reason: Second 2GB check guarantees destination-type sizing (count*desttypesize) stays within int32/tmsize_t on 32-bit systems; only a hypothetical desttypesize==0 from a caller would divide by zero, but callers pass compile-time sizeof constants.

Because target_count64 <= 2147483647/typesize, the uint32 cast cannot truncate a surviving value, datasize = count*typesize cannot wrap and is <= 2147483647, and the checked allocator receives exactly the same (count, typesize) used to compute the copy length — allocation and access sizes are provably equal.

Small-data path copies at most 4 bytes from the 8-byte tdir_offset union (in-bounds); large-data path reads exactly datasize bytes (equal to allocation) via the checked data reader, and frees the buffer on error.
BigTIFF path is symmetric: at most 8 bytes copied from the 8-byte union, and file reads of datasize bytes match the allocation size, with cleanup on read failure.

assumptions: TIFFDataWidth returns 0 for invalid types and at most 8 for valid types, and returns the correct width for tdir_type.
_TIFFCheckMalloc internally validates count*size against TIFF_TMSIZE_T_MAX before allocating.
TIFFReadDirEntryData returns an error on short read / out-of-file offsets rather than partially filling the buffer.
All call sites pass a nonzero compile-time constant for desttypesize (as in upstream libtiff, where callers pass sizeof of a concrete type).
tmsize_t is a signed type at least 32 bits wide, so datasize <= 2147483647 is a valid positive tmsize_t.
limitations: Code for TIFFDataWidth, _TIFFCheckMalloc, TIFFReadDirEntryData, and all callers is not provided, so their safety properties are assumed, not verified.
If a caller could pass desttypesize==0, line 19 would divide by zero (CWE-369); based on upstream libtiff usage this is not reachable, but it cannot be proven from the given code alone.

Only memory safety, integer safety, bounds, and input validation were assessed; higher-level semantic issues (e.g., how callers use *count vs. the truncated file value tdir_count) are out of scope for this function.

verdict.summary: In the version-1.0 ('static short') code path with padding==1, the fill loop skips writing the second byte at every scanline boundary, leaving one uninitialized heap byte per scanline in the g_malloc'd (non-zeroed) buffer; the buffer is then returned to the caller via *data, disclosing uninitialized heap memory when the bitmap is rendered or exported. Additionally, x_hot/y_hot values are accepted without range validation (may be negative or exceed the bitmap dimensions). Buffer bounds themselves are otherwise sound: the %s parses are bounded by the fgets/strlen guard, bytes_per_line is provably even in the version10p path so the 2-byte-stride loop cannot overflow, and the size overflow check catches all wraps of bytes_per_line*hh.

evidence.reason: When padding==1 (version10p and ww%16 in 1..8), the guard ((bytes+2) % bytes_per_line) is false at every scanline end, so the second byte of the last 16-bit unit of each scanline is never written. g_malloc does not zero memory, so one uninitialized heap byte per scanline (hh bytes total) remains in bits; no overflow occurs because bytes_per_line is provably even in this path (ptr advances at most as fast as bytes).

The heap buffer bits is returned via *data without any zeroing or completeness check; in the padding==1 version10p case it contains uninitialized heap bytes (CWE-457/CWE-909 information disclosure through the resulting image). hx/hy come from attacker-controlled '#define x_hot/y_hot' lines and are passed through with no validation against ww/hh or non-negativity.

Hotspot coordinates are assigned directly from the file-controlled 'value' with no range check; negative or out-of-bounds hotspot values are propagated to the caller (CWE-20). Pointer arithmetic is safe only because of short-circuit evaluation of the '||'.

assumptions: g_malloc does not zero the returned block (true for GLib g_malloc).
MAX_SIZE is the same for line and name_and_type and is the literal passed to fgets; the strlen guard therefore bounds every %s token written into name_and_type.
next_int returns a value fitting in int, negative on error, as suggested by the value < 0 check.
init_hex_table/next_int (not shown) behave per their names; only the shown code was analyzed.
The caller treats *data/*width/*height as a fully initialized bitmap, so uninitialized pad bytes are observable output.
limitations: next_int, init_hex_table, MAX_SIZE value, and the caller's use of the returned data were not provided, so downstream impact (exact disclosure vector) is inferred.

The multiplication size = bytes_per_line * hh is unsigned (hh is guint) and the subsequent division check provably catches wraps under wraparound semantics, so it was not flagged as exploitable overflow, though it relies on implementation-defined unsigned-to-int conversion.
sscanf %d on values exceeding INT_MAX is undefined behavior per the C standard; it was not flagged as a primary finding because practical impact here is negligible.
Severity limited to medium because the flaw is an information-exposure/uninitialized-data issue plus weak input validation, not memory corruption.

verdict.summary: No demonstrable security vulnerability in the given code. The unit-list exclusion captures the successor pointer before unlinking, the Item_in_subselect downcast is guarded by a substype() check, and all attacker-relevant pointers are null-checked. The only anomaly is that error-return paths (inner_join->optimize() failure, save_union_explain() failure) skip restoration of lex->current_select and inner_join->select_options, but these paths abort the whole statement before the stale values can be reused, so no use-after-free or other security impact is reachable from this code alone.

evidence.reason: Successor pointer is saved before exclude_level() unlinks/invalidates the unit, and the loop increment prefers next_unit over dereferencing the possibly-stale un. Traversal is correctly ordered; no use-after-unlink.
Downcast to a derived class is guarded by a preceding substype() equality check, so no type confusion is possible.

Early error return skips restoration of lex->current_select and inner_join->select_options (incomplete cleanup, CWE-459 pattern). However, this is a hard-statement-abort path: control returns to the caller for full cleanup that destroys the entire LEX/SELECT_LEX tree, so the stale values are not subsequently dereferenced; no demonstrable use-after-free or security impact follows from the given code.

assumptions: un->thd and un->thd->lex are non-null for attached query units per server invariants; this is internal state, not attacker-controlled input.

Error paths returning TRUE terminate the current statement, after which the caller performs full cleanup of the LEX/SELECT_LEX tree, preventing reuse of the unrestored current_select/select_options values.
exclude_level() may unlink or invalidate the unit, which is why the successor pointer is captured beforehand.
limitations: Only this function was analyzed; callees (exclude_level, save_union_explain, JOIN::optimize, update_used_tables, update_correlated_cache, get_select) are treated as black boxes and could contain vulnerabilities not visible here.

The impact of the unrestored state on error paths depends on caller behavior after the TRUE return, which is not part of the given code; if a caller continued executing with the stale current_select after the error, this could escalate to a use-after-free (CWE-416), but that cannot be established from this snippet alone.
Concurrency behavior (e.g., another thread freeing lex->explain) cannot be assessed from this fragment.

verdict.summary: The checker callback can be bypassed: in the first iterator loop, left_item is assigned before the checker test and is not cleared on failure, so if every item is rejected by the checker, left_item still holds the last (rejected) item and the function proceeds to build and push an equality containing an item the checker explicitly rejected. This enables pushing non-pushable fields into engine conditions, violating the pushdown policy. Secondary risk: when clone_const is false, the const item right_item is aliased directly into the pushed expression (only partially mitigated via IMMUTABLE_FL), and the clones in the const branch do not have set_item_equal(NULL) called, unlike the second loop, leaving stale item_equal back-references.

evidence.reason: left_item is unconditionally assigned before the checker test. If all items fail the checker, the loop exits with left_item pointing at the last rejected item. The subsequent null-check (!left_item) only covers an empty iterator, so the function continues with a checker-rejected item, bypassing the pushdown validation callback (CWE-20/284).

When clone_const is false, the original right_item (not a clone) is embedded in the pushed equality, aliasing one item object across potentially multiple expression trees; the IMMUTABLE_FL walk is only a partial mitigation against double-cleanup/UAF-style misuse.

verdict.summary: SQClass::NewSlot indexes _defaultvalues/_methods with an index read back from the _members table without any bounds validation (lines storing the field/method override). Because Squirrel class inheritance shares the _members table between a base class and its derived classes (and the _locked gate is deliberately bypassed for closures/native closures/bstatic values), an index inserted by a derived class can be interpreted against a base class's smaller _methods/_defaultvalues vectors, producing an out-of-bounds heap write of an SQObjectPtr (including a refcount release on out-of-bounds data, enabling further memory corruption/UAF). The MEMBER_MAX_COUNT check present in this version bounds only growth of new keys; it does not validate indices retrieved from _members. The same shared-table mechanism also yields out-of-bounds reads in class member lookup paths.

evidence.reason: The index _member_idx(temp) is taken from the _members table lookup and used to write into _defaultvalues with no validation that it is < _defaultvalues.size(). The _locked gate was already bypassed for closures (belongs_to_static_table), so this write executes even on locked classes. If _members is shared with a derived class that inserted the key with a frame-relative index larger than this class's vector size, this is an out-of-bounds heap write of an SQObjectPtr (which also releases the out-of-bounds 'old' value's refcount).

Same pattern for the static/method override path: _member_idx(temp) comes from the _members table (which in Squirrel's inheritance design is shared with derived classes) and is used unchecked against _methods.size(). A key added by a derived class with an index valid only in the derived class's frame produces an out-of-bounds write here when NewSlot is invoked on the (locked) base class with a closure or bstatic value.

verdict.summary: startSslClient configures CA trust paths but never enables peer certificate verification (SSL_CTX_set_verify with SSL_VERIFY_PEER is absent and default verify mode is SSL_VERIFY_NONE), and never binds the certificate to the requested hostname (SSL_set_tlsext_host_name only sets SNI, not verification). An active man-in-the-middle can present any certificate and the handshake will succeed. Additionally, the return value of SSL_new is unchecked, so an allocation failure leads to NULL-pointer dereference in SSL_set_options/SSL_set_mode/SSL_set_fd.

evidence.reason: CA trust anchors are loaded, but SSL_CTX_set_verify(ctx, SSL_VERIFY_PEER, ...) is never called anywhere in the function. With the OpenSSL default SSL_VERIFY_NONE, SSL_connect will succeed even if the server presents an invalid, self-signed, or attacker-generated certificate. This permits man-in-the-middle attacks (CWE-295).

The only validation parameter set is X509_V_FLAG_TRUSTED_FIRST (a chain-building strategy hint). X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_host / SSL_set1_host is never called, so the identity in the server's certificate is never checked against 'hostname'. Combined with missing SSL_VERIFY_PEER, hostname mismatch attacks go undetected (CWE-297).

The return value of SSL_new is not checked for NULL. If SSL_new fails, subsequent calls (SSL_set_options, SSL_set_mode, SSL_set_connect_state, SSL_set_fd, SSL_set_tlsext_host_name, SSL_connect) dereference a NULL SSL pointer, causing a crash / denial of service, and the ctx would also be leaked (CWE-476).

evidence.snippet: SSL_set_tlsext_host_name(ssl, hostname.c_str());
evidence.reason: This sets the TLS SNI extension used in the handshake only; it does not configure certificate hostname verification. Return value is also unchecked. Relying on it for identity is a common source of CWE-297.

assumptions: Standard OpenSSL semantics: default verify mode for a new SSL_CTX is SSL_VERIFY_NONE, so client certificate verification is disabled unless explicitly enabled with SSL_CTX_set_verify(SSL_VERIFY_PEER).

SSL_CTX_set1_param duplicates the X509_VERIFY_PARAM, so the trailing X509_VERIFY_PARAM_free does not cause a use-after-free; the errant comment suggesting otherwise does not reflect actual OpenSSL behavior.
SSL_set_tlsext_host_name affects only the SNI extension in the ClientHello, not certificate verification.
limitations: Only this function is analyzed; SSL_CTX_set_verify could theoretically be applied elsewhere (e.g., in a wrapper), but nothing in this code indicates that, and the local X509_VERIFY_PARAM setup strongly suggests verification is intended to be handled here.

verdict.summary: The demuxer trusts parser-computed sizes and non-enforcing asserts for all bounds checks. Multiple paths allow out-of-bounds reads/writes: memcpy into ctx->hdr_store without checking allocation size (remain<5 path), memcpy of 8-bytes_in_header bytes from the input packet that may have fewer than 8 bytes remaining, underflow of remain via start/remain adjustments guarded only by assert() (e.g. remain -= size with size from gf_m4v_parse_frame), negative/huge sizes from pck_size - vosh_start signedness, and pointer arithmetic start + hdr_offset beyond the buffer.

evidence.reason: Copies up to 4 bytes into ctx->hdr_store without verifying hdr_store is allocated or that hdr_store_alloc >= remain. Other paths carefully realloc hdr_store; this one does not, enabling heap overflow or NULL dereference.

evidence.snippet: memcpy(ctx->hdr_store + ctx->bytes_in_header, start, 8 - ctx->bytes_in_header);
evidence.reason: Reads up to 8 bytes from the packet buffer without checking that 'remain' (which can be as low as 5) contains 8 - bytes_in_header bytes; potential out-of-bounds read of the input packet, and assumes hdr_store has capacity >= 8.

size comes from gf_m4v_parse_frame over attacker-controlled bitstream data; the only bounds check is an assert, which is compiled out in release builds. If size > remain, remain underflows and subsequent memcpy/parse iterations read and write out of bounds.

vosh_start is a signed offset into the packet; if it exceeds pck_size (possible after start-code skipping logic), pck_size - vosh_start becomes negative and is cast to size_t/u32, producing a huge length for memcpy — heap buffer overflow. Same pattern repeats in the M4V_VOL_START_CODE case.

evidence.snippet: gf_bs_reassign_buffer(ctx->bs, start + hdr_offset, remain - hdr_offset);
evidence.reason: hdr_offset is computed as 4 - bytes_in_header + current; if current is large relative to remain, remain - hdr_offset underflows (u32/s32 mix) and the bitstream reader is pointed past the end of the packet buffer, causing OOB reads during header parsing.

assumptions: assert() is disabled in release builds (standard NDEBUG configuration), so the assert-based bounds checks provide no protection.
gf_m4v_parse_frame and gf_m4v_parser sizes are derived from parsing the same attacker-controlled data and are not independently bounded here.
hdr_store and hdr_store_alloc start as NULL/0 before first use.
limitations: Helper functions (mpgviddmx_next_start_code, gf_m4v_parse_frame, gf_m4v_parse_config) are not shown, so exact exploitability of each path depends on their internal clamping behavior.
Some arithmetic overflows depend on relationships between vosh_start, pck_size and hdr_store_size that are difficult to trigger without a crafted stream, hence confidence is not 1.0.

verdict.summary: The historical stack-overflow in COPY_BUF is properly guarded (dst bound is checked before each write and cannot be skipped since dst advances by exactly 1 per iteration; block boundaries and EOF are also checked). The remaining weakness in the shown code is an attacker-controlled, effectively unbounded heap allocation: the archive-supplied sparse-map entry count (bounded only by SIZE_MAX) is passed directly to xcalloc before the archive is shown to actually contain that many entries, enabling memory-exhaustion/abort denial of service from a tiny crafted PAX header. Additionally, sp.offset and sp.numbytes are each validated independently up to TYPE_MAXIMUM(off_t) with no combined-overflow check, allowing overflowing extent sums to be registered for downstream extraction.

evidence.snippet: if (!decode_num (&u, nbuf, TYPE_MAXIMUM (size_t))) { ... } file->stat_info->sparse_map_size = u; file->stat_info->sparse_map = xcalloc (file->stat_info->sparse_map_size, sizeof (*file->stat_info->sparse_map));
evidence.reason: The sparse-map entry count is fully attacker-controlled and bounded only by TYPE_MAXIMUM(size_t). It is passed directly to xcalloc with no sanity limit relative to the archive's actual size, so a minimal crafted archive can force an arbitrarily large allocation attempt (memory exhaustion) or an allocation-overflow abort, before any corresponding data is validated.

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; i < file->stat_info->sparse_map_size; i++) { ... decode_num (&u, nbuf, TYPE_MAXIMUM (off_t)) ... sp.offset = u; ... decode_num (&u, nbuf, TYPE_MAXIMUM (off_t)) ... sp.numbytes = u; sparse_add_map (file->stat_info, &sp); }
evidence.reason: Each of sp.offset and sp.numbytes is validated independently up to TYPE_MAXIMUM(off_t); no check prevents offset+numbytes from overflowing off_t. The (potentially overflowing) extent pair is registered in the sparse map and consumed by later extraction logic, an integer-safety (CWE-190) issue whose effect materializes outside this function. The loop itself is correctly bounded by sparse_map_size, so no out-of-bounds write of the map occurs here.

evidence.snippet: if (dst == buf + UINTMAX_STRSIZE_BOUND -1) { ERROR (...numeric overflow in sparse archive member...); return false; } ... *dst = *src++; ... while (*dst++ != '\n'); dst[-1] = 0;
evidence.reason: Mitigating control verified: the destination bound is tested before every write to nbuf, and since dst increments by exactly one per iteration the equality test cannot be stepped over; source pointers are re-bounded at each block boundary with an EOF check. The classic stack buffer overflow in this macro is therefore fixed in the shown version (writes are confined to indices 0..UINTMAX_STRSIZE_BOUND-2).

assumptions: xcalloc is the gnulib allocator: it aborts on size-computation overflow or allocation failure rather than returning a small buffer, so the unbounded allocation leads to exhaustion/abort, not heap corruption.
sparse_add_map appends within the preallocated sparse_map (bounded by sparse_map_size), so the decode loop cannot write past the allocation.
decode_num's third argument is a maximum-value bound, and nbuf is NUL-terminated by dst[-1] = 0 before each decode_num call.
UINTMAX_STRSIZE_BOUND is the declared size of nbuf and is assumed to correctly bound the decimal representation.
limitations: Only the shown function was analyzed; helpers (find_next_block, decode_num, sparse_add_map, set_next_block_after) were assumed to have their documented GNU tar/gnulib semantics.

The offset+numbytes overflow (CWE-190) manifests in downstream extraction code that is not included in the snippet; its exploitability (e.g., wrapped file offsets during extraction) could not be verified here.
The unbounded-allocation finding is denial-of-service grade only; on most configurations the calloc fails or the loop hits archive EOF and tar exits cleanly, so real-world impact is limited.

verdict.summary: The ELF parser trusts every attacker-controlled offset/index from the input file (e_shoff, e_phoff, e_shstrndx, e_shnum, e_phnum, sh_offset, sh_name, d_un.d_val) with no bounds validation against the mapped file size, causing out-of-bounds reads throughout; truncation via strcpy writes '[...]' past the end of the mapping (OOB write); 'dynstr'/'dynamic' are used uninitialized when the sections are absent; and strlen/strcmp/printf %s read past the mapping end. validated_offset checked only the starting pointer 'name', not name+15; writing 6 bytes at name+9 can extend past the end of the mapping, an out-of-bounds write. Additionally strlen(name) itself can read past the mapping end since only the start pointer was validated.

In the section-to-segment mapping loop, 'name' is computed from attacker-controlled values and passed to printf %s with no validated_offset call whatsoever, allowing an out-of-bounds read past the mapping (SIGBUS / information exposure).

dynstr and dynamic are uninitialized if the file has no '.dynstr'/'.dynamic' sections; the uninitialized 'dynamic' is then used as an array index into shdr and its sh_offset/sh_size as mmap offset and loop count, causing use of uninitialized values and out-of-bounds reads.

name = elf_map + shdr[dynstr].sh_offset + dyn[i].d_un.d_val;
snprintf(value, 50, "Shared library: [%s]", name);
evidence.reason: DT_NEEDED's d_un.d_val is a fully attacker-controlled offset applied to the map with no validation, and the resulting pointer is printed with %s, allowing reads far outside the mapped file.
There is no check that st.st_size is at least sizeof(Elf32_Ehdr)/Elf64_Ehdr before dereferencing the header; a truncated or zero-length file causes an immediate out-of-bounds read past the mapping.

if (fstat(fd, &st) < 0) { perror("fstat"); return -1; }
if (elf_map == MAP_FAILED) { perror("mmap"); return -1; }
evidence.reason: All error paths (and the success path) return without close(fd) or munmap, leaking the file descriptor and mapping (CWE-404).

evidence.reason: In the 64-bit path, d_un.d_val is an Elf64_Xword (64-bit) passed to the 32-bit %x conversion, an argument/format type mismatch (undefined behavior, CWE-681).

assumptions: elem is populated by virtqueue_pop with guest-provided descriptor lengths and addresses, per the standard virtio/QEMU VirtQueueElement semantics.

limitations: Only this function is shown; callers of send_control_msg and the definition of virtqueue_pop are not provided, so exploitability of len > in_sg[0].iov_len depends on those implementations (in QEMU this bug is well documented and exploitable by a malicious guest).

verdict.summary: Unbounded write index j into fixed 1024-byte stack buffer szLineConv causes a stack buffer overflow when parsing lines with high-bit/non-UTF-8 characters (each input byte can emit two output bytes). Additional out-of-bounds reads occur from unchecked i increments past len and from the szLine[i+1] look-ahead; the UTF-16 byte-swap loop has no bounds check; szLineConv[i]=0 after wcstombs can write at index 1024; and strcpy copies up to 1024 bytes into a caller-sized szLine.
