verdict.summary: jp2_decode contains several attacker-triggerable memory-safety defects: (1) BPCC component-count mismatch is only warned about, after which bpcs[] is indexed up to the code-stream component count, allowing an out-of-bounds read; (2) in the CMAP path, dec->cdef is dereferenced unconditionally even though a CDEF box need not be present, causing a NULL pointer dereference; (3) the jas_alloc2() result for lutents is never checked before being written; (4) jas_image_depalettize()'s return value is never checked, so a failed depalettize stores an invalid component number in chantocmptlut that is later used to index image components in jas_image_setcmpttype/jas_image_delcmpt; (5) a failed jas_cmprof_createfromiccprof allocation is guarded only by assert().

Attacker-controlled out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

When a CMAP box is present, this code unconditionally computes &dec->cdef->data.cdef, but nothing requires a CDEF box to exist. A crafted file with CMAP+PCLR and no CDEF box leaves dec->cdef NULL, resulting in a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476).

The jas_alloc2() return value is not checked for NULL; the immediately following loop writes through lutents. With attacker-controlled numlutents (PCLR box), an allocation failure leads to a NULL-pointer write (CWE-476 / CWE-251, unchecked allocation).

The return status of jas_image_depalettize() is ignored. If depalettization fails, component newcmptno is never added to the image, yet newcmptno is stored in chantocmptlut and later used to index image components via jas_image_setcmpttype() and jas_image_delcmpt(), causing out-of-bounds/invalid component access (CWE-755, CWE-125).

verdict.summary: status->errormsg, derived from server-supplied SSH_FXP_STATUS data via parse_status_msg, may be NULL and is passed as a %s argument to the printf-style ssh_set_error, causing undefined behavior. Additionally, the response-wait loop has no bound or timeout, allowing a malicious SFTP server to block the client indefinitely.

evidence.snippet:
ssh_set_error(sftp->session, SSH_REQUEST_DENIED,
    "SFTP server: %s", status->errormsg);
evidence.reason: status->errormsg comes from parse_status_msg, which parses server-controlled SSH_FXP_STATUS payloads and may leave errormsg NULL on malformed input. Passing NULL to a printf-style %s is undefined behavior (C standard) and can crash on libc implementations that dereference the argument. There is no NULL check before use.

The loop has no iteration bound, timeout, or nonblocking escape. If the remote SFTP server responds only with messages carrying different request IDs, sftp_dequeue(sftp, id) keeps returning NULL and the loop blocks the calling thread indefinitely, enabling a client-side denial of service by a malicious server.

In the SSH_FX_FAILURE path, the specific FILE_ALREADY_EXISTS error set after a successful lstat is immediately overwritten by the generic ssh_set_error call, defeating the EEXIST mapping. This is a correctness issue rather than a memory-safety flaw, and it also ensures the potentially NULL errormsg path (first evidence item) is always reached on failure.

assumptions: parse_status_msg builds sftp_status_message from server-supplied packet data and can leave errormsg NULL if the payload is malformed; the exact behavior of parse_status_msg is not shown in this snippet.
ssh_set_error is a printf-style variadic formatter that forwards %s arguments to a vsnprintf-like function.
sftp_dequeue(sftp, id) returns NULL when no queued message matches the requested id.
limitations: Definitions of parse_status_msg, sftp_read_and_dispatch, sftp_dequeue, and ssh_set_error are not provided, so the NULL-errormsg and blocking-loop behaviors are inferred from their signatures and call patterns.
Exploitation requires a malicious or compromised SFTP server (or MitM on an unencrypted channel), limiting severity to low.
No memory leaks were found: buffer, path, msg, status, and errno_attr are freed on all exit paths.

verdict.summary: Both the catalog-record type check (thread vs. folder/file) and the node name length check (<= 255, matching the fixed hfsplus_unistr unicode[255] array) are present, which together prevent the historical stack buffer overflow (CVE-2009-4020 pattern) where attacker-controlled disk data could be misinterpreted as a thread record and overflow the search key. Reads into the stack buffer use the full sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry), and the subsequent key build is correctly bounded.

evidence.reason: Type validation prevents file/folder records from being reinterpreted as thread records; without it, attacker-controlled bytes at the thread.nodeName offsets (arbitrary UTF-16 name data) would be used as a length field, enabling an overflow in hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni. This check is present, closing that path.

The length is bounded to 255, exactly the capacity of the fixed unicode[255] array in hfsplus_unirm (HFSPLUS_MAX_STRLEN), so the bounded copy inside hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni stays within fd->search_key. A length of 255 is valid (indices 0..254); no off-by-one.

evidence.reason: The read destination is a full-size hfsplus_cat_entry stack object, so a maximum-size B-tree record cannot overflow the buffer on this read (assuming hfs_brec_read enforces rec_len, which is outside the shown code).

assumptions: hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni copies at most HFSPLUS_MAX_STRLEN (255) UTF-16 code units into fd->search_key, consistent with struct hfsplus_unirm { __be16 length; __be16 unicode[255]; }.
hfs_brec_read rejects records larger than the supplied rec_len (sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry)).
fd->search_key points to a properly sized struct hfsplus_cat_key allocated by the caller (standard kernel HFS+ usage).
limitations: If the on-disk thread record is shorter than the offset of thread.nodeName.length + 2, hfs_brec_read (per its usual implementation) copies only entrylength bytes, potentially leaving the length field and name data uninitialized on the stack before the >255 check reads it; the subsequent use is still bounded, so this is at most a low-severity uninitialized-read issue (CWE-457-class), not a buffer overflow.

Only this function was analyzed; sibling callers in the HFS+ driver may lack equivalent bounds checks and are out of scope.

verdict.summary: mobi_buffer_move performs an out-of-bounds heap read/write via memmove: the negative-offset branch never validates len against buf->maxlen, and the positive-offset branch's bounds check (buf->offset + aoffset + len > buf->maxlen) can be bypassed via size_t integer overflow. Additionally, abs(INT_MIN) is undefined behavior, and buf->offset can be left greater than maxlen after the call.

evidence.reason: Negative-offset branch only verifies buf->offset >= aoffset (source underflow); it never checks that buf->offset + len <= buf->maxlen. With e.g. maxlen=10, buf->offset=5, offset=-1, len=20, memmove copies 20 bytes starting at data+4/data+5, reading and writing ~15 bytes past the end of the heap buffer (CWE-787/CWE-125).

if (buf->offset + aoffset + len > buf->maxlen) { ... return; }
source += aoffset;
evidence.reason: The guard is a size_t sum of three attacker-influenced values (buf->offset, aoffset, len). If the sum wraps modulo 2^64, the check passes and the subsequent memmove reads/writes out of bounds (CWE-190 leading to CWE-787). buf->offset + aoffset can itself overflow before len is added.

evidence.snippet: size_t aoffset = (size_t) abs(offset);
evidence.reason: abs(offset) is undefined behavior when offset == INT_MIN, since the result is not representable as int; the subsequent cast to size_t yields an unspecified huge value (CWE-190).

evidence.snippet: buf->offset += len;
evidence.reason: In the negative-offset branch there is no upper bound on len, so after the call buf->offset can exceed buf->maxlen, corrupting buffer state for all subsequent operations on this MOBIBuffer.

assumptions: MOBIBuffer fields data, offset, maxlen are as inferred from usage; data is a heap allocation of maxlen bytes.
offset and len may be influenced by untrusted file/record data in callers (typical for a MOBI parser library).
size_t is 64-bit and int is 32-bit two's complement on the target platform.
limitations: Callers are not shown; a caller could theoretically pre-validate len, but the function itself performs no such validation and must be safe independently.
No line numbers were provided in the source; line numbers in evidence are counted from the first line of the snippet (1-indexed).

verdict.summary: ZipFile::uncompressEntry extracts archive entries without sanitizing the entry filename, allowing path traversal ('../' segments or absolute paths) so attacker-controlled zip entries can create files, directories, or symlinks (and delete/overwrite existing files) outside the target directory. Attacker-controlled symlink targets further enable link-following escapes when subsequent entries are written. Secondary: getUnchecked(index) performs no bounds check.

evidence.snippet: auto targetFile = targetDirectory.getChildFile (entryPath);
evidence.reason: entryPath comes directly from the zip entry filename and is never checked for '../' traversal segments, absolute paths ('/...' or 'C:\...' on Windows), or UNC paths. getChildFile will resolve these outside targetDirectory, enabling arbitrary file/directory creation outside the intended extraction directory (Zip Slip).

evidence.snippet:
if (entryPath.endsWithChar ('/') || entryPath.endsWithChar ('\\'))
        return targetFile.createDirectory();
evidence.reason: Directory entries also use the unsanitized path, so an entry like '../../somewhere/' creates directories outside the target directory, prepping traversal targets for later entries.

When shouldOverwriteFiles is true, an existing file at the traversed (possibly out-of-sandbox) path is deleted before being replaced with archive-controlled content, escalating traversal to arbitrary file overwrite/deletion.

evidence.snippet:
if (! File::createSymbolicLink (targetFile, originalFilePath, true))
            return Result::fail ("Failed to create symbolic link: " + originalFilePath);
evidence.reason: The symlink target 'originalFilePath' is read from the attacker-controlled archive entry with no validation, and overwrite=true. An attacker can plant a symlink (e.g., to /etc/passwd or another user's file) so that a subsequent entry written through it modifies files outside the extraction directory (symlink-following escape).

evidence.snippet: auto* zei = entries.getUnchecked (index);
evidence.reason: Unchecked array access: if 'index' is attacker/caller-supplied and out of range, this dereferences an out-of-bounds entry pointer (out-of-bounds read / potential null deref), unlike the bounds-checked 'entries[index]' alternative.

assumptions: The entry filename stored in zei->entry.filename originates from untrusted zip archive content.
Typical callers invoke uncompressEntry in a loop over all entries, allowing multi-step traversal/symlink chaining.
File::getChildFile in the underlying framework resolves '..' segments and absolute paths, which is standard behavior for this codebase's File API.
limitations: The implementation of File::getChildFile, createSymbolicLink, and createDirectory is not shown; the traversal/symlink conclusions rely on their standard documented semantics.
Exploitability of getUnchecked depends on whether 'index' can be attacker-influenced at any call site; this function alone does not prove that.

verdict.summary: Use-after-free (read) in the GLOB_TILDE '~user' expansion path: end_name points into the dirname buffer, dirname is freed while malloc_dirname is set, and the freed memory is subsequently read via mempcpy(d, end_name, rest_len). Triggered when glob() is called with GLOB_TILDE, a pattern like '~existinguser/<long path component>/file' whose directory prefix is large enough to force the malloc path (glob_use_alloca false), and the user lookup succeeds. Can yield crashes or disclosure of freed-heap contents in the returned path vector. Secondary: scratch_buffer leaks on several error 'goto out' paths.

evidence.reason: end_name was set via strchr(dirname, '/') and therefore aliases the dirname heap buffer. dirname is freed (when malloc_dirname is set, i.e., when the '~user/...' prefix was large enough that glob_use_alloca returned false), and then rest_len bytes are read from the dangling end_name pointer and copied into the new dirname. This is a heap use-after-free read; freed-chunk metadata (e.g., tcache fd/key) can corrupt the resulting directory string, causing crashes or exposing heap contents through the returned glob results.

Establishes the aliasing precondition: end_name (and unescape) point into the dirname buffer that is later freed in the p != NULL branch, creating the dangling pointer that is dereferenced by mempcpy.

Shows the reachability condition for the UAF: for sufficiently long directory prefixes (alloca threshold exceeded), dirname becomes a heap allocation with malloc_dirname = 1, enabling the later free(dirname) while end_name still references it.
Secondary defect (CWE-401): these 'goto out' paths bypass scratch_buffer_free(&pwtmpbuf), leaking the scratch buffer allocated for the passwd lookup.

assumptions: glob_use_alloca/alloca_account implement the usual glibc behavior: stack allocation only below a size threshold (order of tens of KB), otherwise malloc is used and malloc_dirname is set.
next_brace_sub, glob_in_dir, prefix_array, is_dir, and collated_compare behave as in the corresponding glibc implementation; only the shown function was analyzed.
The environment is POSIX-like (the !WINDOWS32 tilde-expansion branch is compiled in), so the ~user code path is active.
limitations: Helper functions (next_brace_sub, glob_in_dir, prefix_array, is_dir) are not shown and could contain additional issues not covered by this analysis.
Precise line numbers are approximate, derived from counting lines of the provided snippet starting at the function signature.
Exploitability depends on the caller passing attacker-controlled patterns with GLOB_TILDE and on heap state after free; impact ranges from crash to limited heap-content disclosure (read-only UAF).

verdict.summary: hfsplus_find_cat trusts an on-disk catalog thread record after validating only its 2-byte type field. If the record in a corrupted/malicious filesystem image is shorter than sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry), the remainder of the stack buffer 'tmp' (including thread.parentID and thread.nodeName with its length field) is uninitialized stack data that is subsequently consumed by hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni, whose length-driven copy loop is not bounds-checked here, risking use of uninitialized memory and out-of-bounds reads / key-buffer overflow in kernel context.

evidence.reason: 'tmp' is an uninitialized stack buffer; the caller never verifies how many bytes hfs_brec_read actually copied from the on-disk record, nor whether the record length is at least sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry). A short record leaves the tail (parentID, nodeName) as uninitialized stack memory.

evidence.snippet:
type = be16_to_cpu(tmp.type);
if (type != HFSPLUS_FOLDER_THREAD && type != HFSPLUS_FILE_THREAD) { ... return -EIO; }
evidence.reason: The only input validation performed is a 2-byte type check; passing this check does not establish that parentID or nodeName were actually present in the on-disk record, so attacker-controlled disk content bypasses structural validation.

evidence.snippet:
hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni(fd->search_key, be32_to_cpu(tmp.thread.parentID),
			 &tmp.thread.nodeName);
evidence.reason: nodeName is a counted UTF-16 string whose length field comes from untrusted (or, for truncated records, uninitialized) disk data; this function passes it without any bounds check on nodeName.length against the record size or HFSPLUS_MAX_STRLEN, so the callee's length-driven loop can read out of bounds and overflow the key buffer.

assumptions: hfs_brec_read copies the raw on-disk catalog record into 'tmp' based on a length stored in the filesystem image; its implementation is not shown, so it is assumed it does not itself guarantee the record is fully populated within sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry) or that it validates nodeName.length.
hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni iterates over nodeName.length code units and writes into the fixed-size fd->search_key buffer; no clamping is assumed since it is not visible in the provided code.
The catalog B-tree content is attacker-controllable via a crafted HFS+ disk image, the standard threat model for filesystem parsing code.
limitations: The implementations of hfs_brec_read and hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni are not included; if those helpers clamp record lengths and nodeName length to safe bounds, the vulnerability would be reduced to use of uninitialized-but-in-bounds stack data or eliminated entirely.
Actual line numbers are approximate since the snippet was provided without a file/line context.
This is Linux kernel hfsplus code; the true exploitability depends on the kernel version's exact helper implementations.

verdict.summary: This LZW decompressor (gzip unlzw.c) contains the historical hardening fixes: it validates maxbits <= BITS, detects codes exceeding free_ent ('code > free_ent' -> gzip_error), bounds all table accesses by free_ent/maxmaxcode, keeps bit reads within inbuf via the inbits computation, and flushes outbuf with size-checked memcpy. Table-entry invariants (chains strictly descend to <256, prefixes always previously valid codes) prevent de_stack overflow. No reachable memory-safety violation exists in the non-DEBUG build; only a 1-byte debug-only read of inbuf[-1] remains.

evidence.snippet: maxbits &= BIT_MASK; maxmaxcode = MAXCODE(maxbits); if (maxbits > BITS) { ... return ERROR; }
evidence.reason: Input validation of the maxbits header byte bounds all code/table indices to the table capacity; rejects oversized-bit compressed data.

evidence.snippet: inbits = ((rsize != 0) ? ((long)insize - insize%n_bits)<<3 : ((long)insize<<3)-(n_bits-1));
evidence.reason: Bit-stream length is truncated to whole code words so the input() macro never indexes past inbuf.

evidence.snippet: if (code > free_ent) { ... gzip_error (... "corrupt input." ...); }
evidence.reason: Explicit detection of invalid codes beyond the defined table prevents the historical out-of-bounds table read; only code == free_ent (KwKwK) proceeds, starting from oldcode < free_ent.

evidence.snippet: while ((cmp_code_int)code >= (cmp_code_int)256) { *--stackp = tab_suffixof(code); code = tab_prefixof(code); }
evidence.reason: Chain walk is safe: code < free_ent <= maxmaxcode <= MAXCODE(BITS) matches table size, and each entry's prefix is a previously valid oldcode, so chains terminate below 256 and cannot exhaust de_stack.

evidence.snippet: if (outpos+(i = (de_stack-stackp)) >= OUTBUFSIZ) { ... if (i > OUTBUFSIZ-outpos) i = OUTBUFSIZ-outpos; ... memcpy(outbuf+outpos, stackp, i); ... outpos = 0; }
evidence.reason: Output flushing clamps i to remaining buffer space and resets outpos on flush, so memcpy never writes past outbuf.
Minor residual issue: inside #ifdef DEBUG, p[-1] can read one byte before inbuf if posbits>>3 == 0; diagnostic-only, compiled out in normal builds, read-only.

assumptions: Standard gzip definitions of the macros input(), tab_prefixof(), tab_suffixof(), clear_tab_prefixof(), MAXCODE(), and globals inbuf/insize are used, with tables sized for BITS-bit codes.
INBUF_EXTRA is at least large enough that the shift-and-refill logic cannot overflow inbuf (standard gzip invariant).
Non-DEBUG build is being analyzed.
limitations: Definitions of input(), table macros, buffer sizes (INBUFSIZ, OUTBUFSIZ, INBUF_EXTRA), and de_stack sizing are not included in the snippet; the bounds analysis depends on their standard gzip values.
The DEBUG-only inbuf[-1] read is noted but only reachable in debug builds.
This is a data-format parser operating on attacker-controlled input; denial of service via malformed input causing early gzip_error() exit is intended behavior, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: In the USB_DT_OTG handling of composite_setup(), a host-issued GET_DESCRIPTOR(OTG) control request reaches unvalidated source pointers: list_first_entry() is used on cdev->configs with a dead NULL check (empty list yields a bogus container pointer, never NULL), config->descriptors[0] is dereferenced without a NULL check, and the copy length is derived from gadget->otg_caps->otg_rev rather than the actual registered descriptor type, so memcpy() can read past the end of a legacy usb_otg_descriptor (sizeof usb_otg20_descriptor). The over-read bytes are then returned to the host over EP0, enabling kernel information disclosure or a crash/DoS. EP0 destination-buffer bounds are otherwise enforced by the w_length clamp to USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ.

evidence.reason: list_first_entry() never returns NULL; on an empty configs list 'config' is a bogus pointer derived from the list head, making the 'if (!config)' check dead code. The subsequent config->descriptors[0] dereference then reads via an invalid pointer (invalid-object read / crash, DoS).

evidence.snippet:
value = min_t(int, w_length, otg_desc_len);
memcpy(req->buf, config->descriptors[0], value);
evidence.reason: descriptors[0] is not NULL-checked, and the copy length is computed from gadget->otg_caps->otg_rev (sizeof usb_otg20_descriptor when otg_rev >= 0x0200) rather than the actual size of the registered descriptor. If the gadget registered a smaller legacy usb_otg_descriptor (or no descriptors), memcpy over-reads the source object; the bytes are queued to EP0 and disclosed to the host.

Unlike the USB_DT_CONFIG and USB_DT_STRING cases, there is no 'if (value >= 0)' guard on the bos_desc() return before casting to u16; a negative error would be truncated to a large u16 and min() would select w_length, potentially transferring req->buf contents beyond what bos_desc() initialized (secondary, depends on bos_desc error behavior).

assumptions: USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ matches the allocated size of cdev->req->buf and USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ matches cdev->os_desc_req->buf, so the w_length clamps make destination writes safe.

Gadget drivers may register configurations whose descriptors[] entries are NULL or that omit an OTG descriptor.

verdict.summary: Analysis shows all pointer accesses are bounds-checked: fast loop's 10-increment skip is bounded by the 11*len reserve (tp[-1] reads stay <= text+size-1), the memchr heuristic decrements tp before computing the length and re-checks 'ep <= tp' to break, bm_delta2_search receives ep as a hard end bound, and the final slow loop guards reads with 'd <= ep - tp' so tp[-1] never exceeds text[size-1]. Early guards handle len==0, len>size, and len==1. No out-of-bounds read, write, integer overflow, or infinite loop found. This matches the fixed version of grep's bmexec_trans; however, full confirmation depends on internals of bm_delta2_search and memchr_kwset, which are not shown.

if (size > 12 * len)

evidence.reason: Fast loop is entered only when size > 12*len; ep = text + size - 11*len leaves an 11*len reserve so the ten bounded increments (d <= len each) keep tp <= text + size - len, keeping all tp[-1] reads in bounds.

The decrement before computing the memchr length keeps the byte count >= 0 and <= size, the NULL check exits safely, and the 'ep <= tp' break prevents the loop body from running with tp beyond the reserved region — this is the bounds fix for the historical OOB in this heuristic.
Slow loop bounds: the loop condition 'd <= ep - tp' ensures tp <= ep before/after increments, so tp[-1] <= text[size-1]; the pre-loop read is safe because tp <= text+size on every path reaching it.

The U() macro casts its argument to unsigned char, preventing negative indices into d1.
bm_delta2_search internally clamps tp against its ep argument and returns a match position within [text, ep - len], and memchr_kwset behaves like memchr bounded by its length argument.
kwset->mind (len), kwset->target, kwset->delta, and kwset->gc1/gc2 are consistent with the built kwset (built by the same library).
limitations: bm_delta2_search, memchr_kwset, the U() macro, and kwset construction code are not shown; the non-vulnerable verdict for those components is assumed from their contracts and cannot be verified from the given code alone.

verdict.summary: printIFDStructure computes the buffer size as size*count in uint32_t arithmetic, which wraps for attacker-controlled type/count (e.g., 4-byte type with count=0x40000000 yields a ~20-byte buffer). For XMP/ICC tags, kount is set to the full un-wrapped count, so buf.pData_[count]=0 is a heap out-of-bounds write, out.write(buf.pData_,count) and Internal::binaryToString(buf,kount) are out-of-bounds reads. Additionally, the next-IFD offset and sub-IFD/MakerNote offsets are used unvalidated (the bounds check is commented out), enabling an infinite do/while loop and unbounded self-recursion (stack exhaustion).

evidence.snippet: uint32_t size   = isStringType(type) ? 1 ... : 8 : 1; DataBuf  buf(size*count + pad+20);
evidence.reason: size and count are both uint32_t; size*count wraps modulo 2^32. A crafted IFD entry (e.g., 4-byte type with count=0x40000000, or 8-byte type with count=0x20000000) makes the product wrap to 0, so buf is allocated with only pad+20 bytes while count remains huge. bOffsetIsPointer (count*size > 4) is also evaluated on the wrapped value.

evidence.snippet: if ( isPrintXMP(tag,option) ) { buf.pData_[count]=0; out << (char*) buf.pData_; }
evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds write: the write index is the un-wrapped attacker-controlled count while the buffer was sized with the wrapped (near-zero) size*count. isPrintXMP depends only on tag/option, so an XMP tag with a 4/8-byte type triggers this. Classic integer-overflow-to-heap-overflow (CWE-190 -> CWE-122/787).

evidence.snippet: if ( isPrintICC(tag,option) ) { out.write((const char*)buf.pData_,count); }
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: count bytes are written to the output stream from a buffer allocated with the wrapped (tiny) size*count + pad + 20, e.g., ICC tag 0x8773 with an 8-byte type and count=0x20000000 reads ~512MB from a 20-byte heap buffer.

evidence.snippet: uint32_t kount  = isPrintXMP(tag,option) ? count : isPrintICC(tag,option) ? count
evidence.reason: For XMP/ICC tags kount equals the full (un-wrapped) count, and Internal::binaryToString(buf, kount) (line 104) iterates that many bytes over the wrapped-small buffer, an out-of-bounds read on the same trigger paths.

evidence.snippet: if ( start ) { io.read(dir.pData_, 4); start = tooBig ? 0 : byteSwap4(dir,0,bSwap); } } while (start) ;
evidence.reason: The next-IFD offset is read from the file and used without any validation (the check 'if ( offset > io.size() ) offset = 0;' is deliberately commented out at line 64). An IFD whose next-offset points back to itself makes the do/while loop iterate forever: CPU denial of service (CWE-835).

evidence.snippet: if ( option == kpsRecursive && (tag == 0x8769 || tag == 0x014a || type == tiffIfd) ) { for ( size_t k = 0 ; k < count ; k++ ) { ... printIFDStructure(io,out,option,offset,bSwap,c,depth); ... } }
evidence.reason: Uncontrolled recursion with attacker-controlled offsets: the function calls itself for each SubIFD/ExifIFD entry and depth is incremented but never bounded. A cyclic or deeply chained IFD graph exhausts the stack (CWE-674). The same applies to the MakerNote branch (lines 141-144).

evidence.snippet: // if ( offset > io.size() ) offset = 0; // Denial of service? ... io.seek(offset,BasicIo::beg); io.read(buf.pData_,count*size);
evidence.reason: offset is never validated against the stream size, and the return values of io.seek/io.read are never checked. Seeks/reads past EOF leave the buffer with stale/uninitialized content that is subsequently printed, and huge valid count values (without wrap) cause oversized allocations (std::bad_alloc DoS).

assumptions: typeValid(type) restricts size to values in {1,2,4,8} as encoded in the size selection chain.
isPrintXMP/isPrintICC depend on tag and option only, not on the entry's type, so their tags can carry 4- or 8-byte types.
uint32_t arithmetic (size*count, count*size) wraps modulo 2^32 per standard C++ semantics.
The caller can invoke this with kpsRecursive to reach the recursion branches; attacker fully controls the TIFF/EXIF byte stream.
limitations: Exact semantics of DataBuf (zero-initialization), byteSwap2/byteSwap4, and the BasicIo seek/read failure behavior are not shown; if reads past EOF fail safely and DataBuf zero-initializes, the info-leak aspect is mitigated but the OOB write/read, recursion, and infinite-loop findings stand.
The overflow-to-OOB requires count*size to wrap; exact exploitability (offset reachability for the write index) depends on heap layout, but the OOB is reachable by construction.
Internal::binaryToString, IptcData::printStructure, printTiffStructure, and typeValid implementations are not provided; their internal safety is out of scope.

verdict.summary: No memory-corruption flaw was found in the shown pixel-decoding paths (strides match allocations, colormap indices are validated), but two reachable defects remain: (1) the quantum_bits mask-scanning loops use a '> 32' guard, allowing a left shift of a 32-bit mask by 32 (undefined behavior) with attacker-controlled BI_BITFIELDS masks (e.g. 0x001F/0xFFFF), and (2) the multi-image BA loop seeks to file-controlled ba_offset values with only a single-frame offset_bits repeat check, so a crafted 2-cycle of BA blocks causes an infinite loop that appends decoded images to the image list without bound (unbounded memory/CPU). Additionally, bmp_info fields such as alpha_mask are not reset per frame, allowing stale cross-frame data to affect alpha handling.

evidence.reason: For a mask with bits contiguous down to bit 0 (e.g. blue_mask=0x001F used by standard RGB555, or 0xFFFFFFFF via BI_BITFIELDS), sample reaches 32; the guard is 'sample > 32' (not '>= 32'), so the loop condition evaluates 'mask << 32' on a 32-bit type, which is undefined behavior (CWE-758). Attacker-reachable via the 16/32-bit BI_BITFIELDS code path; benign on mainstream hardware but non-conforming.

ba_offset is a fully file-controlled seek target. The only loop protection is 'if (bmp_info.offset_bits == offset_bits)' which compares only against the previous frame. A crafted file containing two BA blocks whose ba_offsets reference each other, with two interleaved sub-images having distinct offset_bits values (A,B,A,B,...), passes every per-frame validation forever: seeks remain inside the file (so EOFBlob never fires), number_scenes is 0 by default, and each iteration calls AcquireNextImage, appending a fully decoded image. Result: infinite loop with unbounded image-list/pixel-cache growth (CWE-835, CWE-400).

evidence.snippet:
start_position=TellBlob(image)-2;
bmp_info.ba_offset=0;
evidence.reason: Only bmp_info.ba_offset is reset at the top of each multi-image iteration. Fields such as alpha_mask (read only when bmp_info.size > 40) persist across frames: a subsequent frame with a 40-byte BITMAPINFOHEADER inherits the previous frame's alpha_mask, which can incorrectly enable image->matte and select a stale alpha mask for pixel extraction. Stale-data/correctness issue, not memory-unsafe.

assumptions: ReadBlob/ReadBlobLSB*/SeekBlob behave as in ImageMagick core: SeekBlob to arbitrary in-file offsets succeeds, ReadBlob returns the number of bytes actually read.
IsValidColormapIndex sets a safe (clamped/zero) index on failure, so colormap index writes cannot go out of range.
AcquireVirtualMemory detects count*quantum overflow, and SetImageExtent enforces resource limits, bounding columns/rows to sane values.
DecodeImage (not shown) is assumed to bound its writes by the number_pixels argument passed as image->columns*image->rows; the shown call site allocates a buffer >= that product.
Shifts behave with x86-style masking in practice, so the 'mask << 32' UB does not corrupt memory on mainstream platforms.
limitations: DecodeImage, IsBMP, SeekBlob, QueueAuthenticPixels and AcquireVirtualMemory implementations are not shown; RLE decode overflows inside DecodeImage cannot be ruled out from this snippet alone.
Line numbers in evidence are approximate since the snippet was provided without a line-numbered file.
The cyclic-BA-offset DoS depends on SeekBlob accepting backward in-file seeks and on IsBMP recognizing 'BA' magic, both consistent with ImageMagick behavior but not shown here.

verdict.summary: In the 'last descriptor' path, desc_first is DMA-read and DMA-written with sizeof(desc_first) (DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS * 4 bytes) regardless of the actual configured descriptor length (4 * gem_get_desc_len(s,false)), causing out-of-bounds reads and writes of guest memory adjacent to the first TX descriptor, including writing stale stack data into guest RAM. The packet-gather bounds check itself is sound.

evidence.reason: DMA access size uses sizeof(desc_first) (DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS*4 bytes) instead of the actual descriptor size used everywhere else (sizeof(uint32_t)*gem_get_desc_len(s,false)). With a guest-configured 2-word (or 4-word) descriptor layout, this reads and writes up to 16/8 bytes past the first descriptor's bounds: an out-of-bounds DMA read (CWE-125) and out-of-bounds DMA write (CWE-787) of guest memory, plus writeback of stale stack bytes.

Guest-controlled descriptor data is read into fixed stack buffer desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS]. Safe only if gem_get_desc_len can never exceed DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS for TX (assumed 2 or 4); if guest-configurable register state could yield a larger value, this would be a stack buffer overflow. Also, the address_space_read return status is ignored.

evidence.snippet:
if (tx_desc_get_length(desc) > gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) -
                                   (p - s->tx_packet)) { ... break; }
evidence.reason: Bounds check for the gather buffer. Traced pointer arithmetic shows p never exceeds the buffer while fragments are accepted (unsigned subtraction is safe because p - s->tx_packet <= buffer size by induction), so the tx_packet gather path is NOT overflowable — the primary defect is elsewhere (desc_first handling).

assumptions: gem_get_desc_len(s,false) returns 2 or 4 (TX descriptors), never exceeding DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS; the definitions of gem_get_desc_len, DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS, gem_get_max_buf_len, and the size of s->tx_packet are not present in the given code.
address_space_read/write operate on guest DMA address space and clamp to mapped memory regions, so the OOB access corrupts guest RAM adjacent to the descriptor rather than emulator process memory.
GEM register state (NWCTRL, DMACFG, descriptor words) is fully guest-controlled, which is the attacker input surface.
limitations: Helper functions (gem_get_desc_len, gem_get_max_buf_len, tx_desc_* accessors) are not shown, so exact overflow magnitude and the stack-overflow potential of the desc read cannot be fully confirmed.

The severity assumes the QEMU device-emulation threat model: guest-triggerable OOB DMA read/write of guest memory adjacent to the descriptor; direct QEMU host-process memory corruption via this path is unlikely because the stack buffer desc_first is large enough for the read and address_space_write targets guest address space.

address_space_read failure handling (unmapped descriptor addresses leaving stale desc content) may enable descriptor reprocessing but was not verifiable without the address_space_read semantics in this code version.

verdict.summary: ZipFile::uncompressEntry performs an unchecked out-of-bounds array access via entries.getUnchecked(index) with no validation of the caller-supplied index, has a TOCTOU race between the path/symlink checks and file creation, and, when followSymlinks is yes, creates attacker-controlled symlinks with overwrite=true, enabling writes outside the target extraction directory.

evidence.snippet: auto* zei = entries.getUnchecked (index);
evidence.reason: The caller-supplied 'index' is never bounds-checked against entries.size() before getUnchecked dereferences the array. An out-of-range index yields an out-of-bounds read of a raw pointer which is dereferenced immediately (zei->entry...), causing undefined behavior in release builds (crash or memory disclosure). CWE-125/CWE-787.

evidence.snippet: if (! targetFile.isAChildOf (targetDirectory)) ... if (! targetFile.deleteFile()) ... if (followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::no && hasSymbolicPart (...)) ... FileOutputStream out (targetFile);
evidence.reason: All path-containment and symlink checks (isAChildOf, hasSymbolicPart) are evaluated before the filesystem is mutated (deleteFile, createDirectory, FileOutputStream). A local attacker can replace a parent directory component with a symlink between the check and the write, causing FileOutputStream to write outside targetDirectory. Check-time/use-time race, CWE-367/CWE-59.

evidence.snippet: if (zei->entry.isSymbolicLink) { String originalFilePath (in->readEntireStreamAsString()...); if (! File::createSymbolicLink (targetFile, originalFilePath, true)) ... }
evidence.reason: The symlink destination is taken verbatim from the archive entry content with no validation, and createSymbolicLink is called with overwrite=true. When followSymlinks is yes, an attacker-crafted archive can place a symlink to an absolute path (e.g., /etc/...) inside the extraction directory; subsequent entries traversing it write outside the target directory (symlink-based Zip Slip, CWE-59). The hasSymbolicPart guard only applies when FollowSymlinks::no is selected.

evidence.snippet: auto targetFile = targetDirectory.getChildFile (entryPath); if (! targetFile.isAChildOf (targetDirectory)) return Result::fail (...);
evidence.reason: Path traversal via entryPath is mitigated only insofar as JUCE's File::getChildFile/isAChildOf normalize and compare lexically (their implementations are not shown). The check is string-based and does not resolve symlinks, so containment depends entirely on the hasSymbolicPart check and the caller passing FollowSymlinks::no; it does not protect against runtime filesystem races.

assumptions: JUCE semantics assumed: Array::getUnchecked performs no runtime bounds check in release builds; File::getChildFile lexically normalizes '..' components; File::isAChildOf is a lexical prefix-based comparison; File::createSymbolicLink's third argument is an overwrite flag.
Entry metadata (filename, isSymbolicLink, fileTime) is fully attacker-controlled when the ZipFile is opened from untrusted input.
This snippet appears to be a post-Zip-Slip-fix JUCE version, since explicit traversal and symlink checks are present.
limitations: Implementations of entries.getUnchecked, File::getChildFile, File::isAChildOf, hasSymbolicPart, and File::createSymbolicLink are not shown; severity of the OOB access and effectiveness of the traversal guard depend on those implementations.
Exploitability of the TOCTOU race requires a local attacker or concurrent process able to modify parent directories during extraction.
The symlink-based escape via FollowSymlinks::yes may be considered intended caller-configurable behavior; it is a vulnerability primarily when untrusted archives are extracted with that option.

verdict.summary: The reader applies layered validation (bits_per_sample 1..32, samples_per_pixel<=32, colormap size matched to 2^bits_per_sample, HeapOverflowSanityCheck, scanline-to-buffer 1.5x sanity check with MagickMax reallocation, and per-strip/tile pointer resets), and all decode methods' read lengths are bounded by their respective allocations. No concrete vulnerability is reachable from the given code on 64-bit builds; residual risks are theoretical 32-bit size_t overflow in extent computations (4*(samples_per_pixel+1)*TIFFStripSize) and reliance on libtiff array-size contracts for sample_info/colormap.

assumptions: Target platform is 64-bit (size_t and libtiff tmsize_t are 64-bit), which is the mainstream ImageMagick build.

libtiff honors its field contracts: TIFFTAG_COLORMAP arrays contain 1<<BitsPerSample entries, TIFFTAG_EXTRASAMPLES sample_info array contains at least extra_samples entries, and TIFFReadEncodedStrip/TIFFReadTile write at most the sizes passed.
SetImageExtent and AcquireMagickResource enforce dimension/resource limits before the decode loops.
limitations: On 32-bit builds, extent=4*(samples_per_pixel+1)*TIFFStripSize(tiff) and rows*TIFFTileRowSize(tiff) could overflow size_t, potentially producing an undersized heap buffer prior to TIFFReadEncodedStrip/TIFFReadTile writes (CWE-190/CWE-122); this could not be confirmed without target platform details.

number_pixels uses floating point (pow/log); precision loss for extreme dimensions is theoretically possible, though the scanline_size > 1.5*number_pixels rejection plus MagickMax(scanline_size, number_pixels) anchoring prevents an undersized scanline buffer.
Behavior of external libtiff functions (TIFFReadPixels, TIFFReadRGBAImage, colormap sizing) is assumed per libtiff documentation; a nonconforming or vulnerable libtiff would change the analysis.

verdict.summary: This is the hardened (post-CVE-fix) version of libtiff's LZWDecodeCompat. All output writes are bounded by occ/residue; table reads/writes are guarded by explicit range checks on free_entp, free_entp->next (the oldcodep sentinel), and the codep->length == 0 check; code indices are bounded by the 12-bit nbitsmask < CSIZE. No input-reachable memory-safety violation is constructible from the code as given, provided the standard surrounding libtiff invariants hold.

evidence.reason: Bounds checks on the free-entry pointer and on oldcodep (which may be the pre-table sentinel &dec_codetab[-1]) are performed before any table write or dereference, closing the historical heap out-of-bounds write/read (CVE-2016-3623 class) in this function.
Rejects codes that reference undefined/zeroed table entries before the reverse-copy loop; without this check, a zero-length entry would cause *--tp to write one byte before the output buffer.

Restart path: the skip loop terminates at a base entry (length 1 <= occ, occ > 0 guaranteed by the outer loop), so no NULL dereference; exactly occ bytes are written into op[0..occ-1]; the dec_restart/dec_codep invariant (dec_restart < dec_codep->length) is maintained, keeping the next call's residue positive and bounded.

When length <= occ, the reverse copy writes exactly codep->length bytes, which equals the number of chain nodes (derived entries: length = next->length+1; base entries: length 1, next NULL), so the loop is bounded by both the buffer and the chain.
nbits is clamped to BITS_MAX (12), so codes read via NextCode are masked to <= 4095 < CSIZE; codep = dec_codetab + code remains in-bounds and nbitsmask/maxcodep cannot grow past the table.

assumptions: CSIZE = MAXCODE(BITS_MAX)+1 = 4096 and dec_codetab has CSIZE entries.
NextCode/GetNextCodeCompat mask the read code to nbitsmask (nbits <= 12), so code <= 4095 < CSIZE.
Base entries 0..255 are initialized with length 1 and next NULL; entries [CODE_FIRST, CSIZE) are zeroed at setup and at CODE_CLEAR.
dec_oldcodep starts as the sentinel &dec_codetab[-1] before the first code of a strip; the free_entp->next range check rejects it.
dec_restart is only assigned values < dec_codep->length (<= ~4096), so no integer truncation is reachable regardless of its declared type.
limitations: The NextCode/GetNextCodeCompat macros, LZWSetupDecode, and the code_t/LZWCodecState definitions are not shown; the verdict depends on the stated invariants (in particular EOF/EOS handling and that LZW_CHECKEOS yields CODE_EOI when input is exhausted).
assert() statements are inert when NDEBUG is defined, but the guarded conditions here are redundant with explicit checks or loop bounds.

The function historically contained exploitable out-of-bounds writes/reads (e.g., CVE-2016-3623); this analysis finds those exact paths closed by the checks present in the given code, but a vulnerability introduced in unshown callers or macros cannot be excluded.

verdict.summary: This libcurl header callback parses response data that is not NUL-terminated. The sscanf(input, "%u\r\n", &limit) call can read past the end of the delivered buffer when the timelimit header value is empty or whitespace-only, because %u skips leading whitespace including the terminating CRLF and keeps scanning adjacent heap memory (CWE-125). Secondary issues: unchecked size*nmemb multiplication (CWE-190), unchecked dereferences of client->auth, auth->state and client->con (CWE-476), and a possible time_t overflow at time(NULL) + limit. The icecast-auth-message memcpy path is correctly bounds-checked (len > 24 guard, clamp to sizeof(errormsg), CRLF validation), so no overflow there.

evidence.snippet: if (sscanf(input, "%u\r\n", &limit) == 1) {
evidence.reason: input points into the libcurl header buffer, which per the CURLOPT_HEADERFUNCTION contract is not NUL-terminated, and only len bytes are valid. scanf's %u conversion skips leading whitespace, and '\r'/'\n' are whitespace. If the backend sends the timelimit header with an empty or whitespace-only value (e.g. 'icecast-user-timelimit:\r\n'), sscanf consumes the terminating CRLF validated at line 18 and continues reading bytes beyond ptr+len-1, i.e. past the end of the delivered data and potentially past the heap allocation. This is an attacker-influenceable (via auth backend response) buffer over-read.

evidence.snippet: size_t len = size * nmemb;
evidence.reason: Unchecked multiplication of attacker/caller-supplied size and nmemb can overflow size_t (CWE-190/680), producing a truncated len. In practice libcurl invokes the header callback with size == 1, which prevents overflow, but the function performs no check of its own; any caller violating that contract gets mis-scaled bounds checks for all downstream logic.

evidence.snippet:
auth_t *auth = client->auth;
        auth_url *url = auth->state;
evidence.reason: Only auth_user->client is NULL-checked (line 7). client->auth and auth->state are dereferenced without validation; similarly client->con is dereferenced at line 22 (client->con->discon_time). If any of these is NULL (e.g. a client whose auth state was torn down), the function dereferences NULL, causing a crash (CWE-476).

evidence.snippet: client->con->discon_time = time(NULL) + limit;
evidence.reason: limit is an unvalidated unsigned int parsed from the backend response (up to 4294967295). Adding it to time(NULL) can overflow/wrap a 32-bit time_t, yielding a discon_time in the past (immediate client disconnect) instead of the intended future time; unchecked addition on externally supplied value (CWE-190, minor).

assumptions: ptr points to a libcurl header callback buffer that is not NUL-terminated and contains exactly len valid bytes (documented libcurl CURLOPT_HEADERFUNCTION behavior).
url->auth_header_len and url->timelimit_header_len equal strlen() of their respective non-NULL header strings (configured consistently elsewhere), so strncasecmp reads are in-bounds.
url->errormsg is a fixed-size array (sizeof yields its capacity, not a pointer size).

The auth backend URL is admin-configured, so the header content is semi-trusted; the over-read requires the backend (or something influencing it, e.g. via reflection of listener input) to emit a malformed timelimit header.
limitations: Struct definitions, configuration code that sets auth_header_len/timelimit_header_len, and errormsg's declaration are not provided, so exact sizes and the header-length consistency cannot be verified from the given code alone.

Actual over-read past a heap allocation depends on libcurl's internal buffer layout; reading past the line's CRLF may remain inside curl's allocation in many cases, so exploitability (crash vs. silent parse) varies by curl version and response position.

The icecast-auth-message memcpy path was case-analyzed (len=25 minimum, clamped copy_len == sizeof(errormsg), unclamped boundary) and found correctly bounded; this was not flagged as an evidence item.
No dynamic testing or compilation was performed; the analysis is a static control-flow/bounds trace of the given code only.

verdict.summary: GmfOpenMesh leaks the mesh structure and its open file handle/fd when ScaKwdTab fails (bypassing the longjmp cleanup path), dereferences the unchecked FilNam argument, and writes through unchecked caller-supplied PtrVer/PtrDim pointers; the ASCII parsing loop also performs a conditional stack buffer overflow via fscanf("%100s") if GmfStrSiz < 101.

evidence.reason: strlen(FilNam) is called with no NULL check; a NULL FilNam causes a NULL-pointer dereference (crash/DoS). The subsequent strcpy itself is bounds-checked and safe for non-NULL inputs.

fscanf writes up to 100 characters plus a NUL terminator into str[GmfStrSiz]. The code shown does not establish GmfStrSiz >= 101; if GmfStrSiz is smaller, a stack buffer overflow (CWE-787) occurs with file-controlled data. Also, if fscanf returns 0 (matching failure), strcmp reads an indeterminate buffer.

Caller-supplied output pointers are extracted from varargs with no validation; later writes (*PtrVer) = msh->ver; (*PtrDim) = msh->dim; dereference them unconditionally, allowing a NULL or invalid pointer write (CWE-476).

This early return bypasses the setjmp-based cleanup handler used by every other failure path: the calloc'd msh structure is leaked and the open FILE*/file descriptor (msh->hdl or msh->FilDes) is never closed. Triggerable by an attacker-supplied/corrupted mesh file, enabling memory and file-descriptor exhaustion (CWE-401/CWE-772).

assumptions: GmfStrSiz, WrdSiz, GmfRead/GmfWrite, safe_fread, safe_fscanf, ScaWrd, RecWrd, GetPos, ScaKwdTab and the GmfMshSct layout are defined elsewhere and not shown.
msh->FilNam is declared with size GmfStrSiz in the (unseen) struct, making the strcpy bounds check meaningful.
Line numbers are approximations derived from counting the code as presented.
limitations: GmfStrSiz's actual value is unknown; the fscanf overflow (width 100) is conditional on GmfStrSiz < 101 (in the real libMeshb it is large, which would neutralize that finding).
Behavior of the not-shown helpers (ScaKwdTab, ScaWrd, RecWrd, GetPos, safe_fread/safe_fscanf) cannot be audited and may contain additional vulnerabilities.
Casting a pointer to int64_t (MshIdx) is lossy on hypothetical >64-bit pointers, but this is not an issue on mainstream platforms.
Severity assumes a non-malicious caller for the varargs pointers; the FilNam NULL and ScaKwdTab leak findings hold even for benign inputs.

verdict.summary: php_wddx_pop_element processes attacker-controlled WDDX XML and (1) dereferences ent2->data via Z_TYPE_P without a general NULL check (only ST_FIELD NULL entries are guarded, while NULL-data stack entries demonstrably exist), (2) decrements ent1->data's refcount with Z_DELREF_P before an unchecked add_property_zval call, risking premature free/UAF, (3) invokes attacker-influenced __wakeup() code re-entrantly while the parser stack holds raw pointers to mid-construction values, (4) pops entries in the EL_FIELD branch without verifying entry type, freeing data/varname leaks and allowing parser stack desynchronization, and (5) leaks ent1->varname and ent1->data on several early-return/non-container paths.

evidence.reason: Proves NULL-data stack entries exist. On this early-return path ent1->varname is never freed (memory leak, CWE-401), and the tag name is trusted without verifying it matches the entry type on top of the stack.

Arbitrary user-defined PHP code (__wakeup on an attacker-chosen class) executes during deserialization while the parser stack holds raw pointers to partially built values (ent1, ent2->data, stack entries), a re-entrancy / use-after-free hazard (CWE-416) and an unsafe-deserialization gadget surface (CWE-502).

Only ST_FIELD entries are NULL-checked; the subsequent Z_TYPE_P(ent2->data) dereferences ent2->data for all other entry types, so any other NULL-data entry on the stack causes a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476), crash/DoS from malformed input.

The refcount of ent1->data is decremented before add_property_zval, whose return value is never checked. If insertion fails (e.g., a __set handler or error path), the zval can be freed while still referenced, yielding a use-after-free (CWE-416).

The top entry is freed and popped without verifying it is actually an ST_FIELD entry, without freeing ent->data or ent->varname. A malformed document can pop an arbitrary entry, desynchronizing the parser stack and leaking tracked values (CWE-401, state confusion).

assumptions: wddx_stack_top returns the top entry when stack->top > 0 (guaranteed by the initial guard).
This is the historical PHP ext/wddx deserializer callback driven by expat on attacker-supplied XML; ent1->varname, element names, and class names all originate from the untrusted document.
Stack entries other than ST_FIELD can hold data == NULL, as demonstrated by the explicit !ent1->data branch at the top of the value-element path.
limitations: Helper implementations (wddx_stack_top, php_wddx_push_element, zend_symtable_update, add_property_zval) are not shown, so exact reachability of the NULL-deref and UAF paths cannot be proven from this snippet alone.
Whether ent1->varname can alias stack->varname (double free) depends on php_wddx_push_element, which is not included.
Severity of the __wakeup re-entrancy issue depends on PHP engine internals (zval refcounting) not shown here.

verdict.summary: Bounds checks in mobi_buffer_move use unchecked size_t additions (buf->offset + aoffset + len, buf->offset + len) that can wrap around SIZE_MAX, bypassing the guards and causing out-of-bounds read/write in memmove. Additionally, abs(offset) is undefined behavior when offset == INT_MIN, corrupting the aoffset used in all subsequent checks.

evidence.snippet: size_t aoffset = (size_t) abs(offset);
evidence.reason: abs(INT_MIN) is undefined behavior in C; the resulting aoffset is unreliable and is used in every subsequent bounds check, potentially defeating both start- and end-of-buffer protections.

evidence.snippet: if (buf->offset + aoffset + len > buf->maxlen) { ... return; }
evidence.reason: size_t addition can overflow (wrap around SIZE_MAX) when offset/len are attacker-influenced, causing the guard to pass despite the region extending beyond buf->maxlen; source is then advanced by aoffset and memmove performs an out-of-bounds read (source) and write (destination).

evidence.snippet: if ( (buf->offset < aoffset) || (buf->offset + len > buf->maxlen) ) { ... return; }
evidence.reason: The end-of-buffer check buf->offset + len can also wrap for very large len, bypassing the guard; the following memmove writes len bytes at data + buf->offset, overflowing the heap buffer. The start check buf->offset < aoffset additionally depends on the UB-derived aoffset.

evidence.snippet: memmove(buf->data + buf->offset, source, len); buf->offset += len;
evidence.reason: Both operands are validated only by the overflowable checks above; under wrapped-sum conditions this memmove reads and writes out of bounds (CWE-125/CWE-787), and buf->offset += len can itself overflow, corrupting subsequent buffer state.

assumptions: buf->data, buf->maxlen, and buf->offset are assumed to be well-formed and internally consistent before the call (i.e., 0 <= buf->offset <= buf->maxlen and buf->data is valid for maxlen bytes).
offset and len (or the data from which they derive) are assumed to be at least partially attacker-influenced, as is typical for parsers of untrusted input.
size_t is assumed to be 64-bit or 32-bit per platform; overflow of size_t additions is possible on either when operands are large enough.
limitations: No concrete caller code or input source is provided, so exploitability (e.g., whether len can realistically approach values that trigger wraparound) is inferred rather than demonstrated.
The analysis assumes two's complement / standard C semantics for size_t wraparound; exact behavior of abs(INT_MIN) is undefined and platform-dependent.
Only the shown function was analyzed; whether upstream callers independently constrain offset/len could reduce practical severity but cannot be verified from the given code.

verdict.summary: The function matches the fixed upstream Linux implementation of esp6_output_head(). All trailer/appended-data writes are bounded (tailroom check, page_frag refill sized >= tailen, trailer fill = tfclen+plen+2 = tailen bytes), the MAX_SKB_FRAGS guard prevents the historical skb_shared_info frags[] out-of-bounds write, the x->lock is correctly released on all paths (including the refill-failure goto cow), and the stale esp->esph pointer after skb_cow_data is handled by recomputing it from the saved esph_offset. No memory-safety, bounds, integer, lifetime, or locking flaw is reachable from the shown control flow.

evidence.snippet:
} else if ((skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS)
		   && !skb_has_frag_list(skb)) {
evidence.reason: Bounds check present before __skb_fill_page_desc/skb_shinfo nr_frags increment; prevents the known out-of-bounds write into skb_shared_info.frags[] when nr_frags == MAX_SKB_FRAGS. This guard is the historical security fix and is intact here.

The ESP header pointer, which can be invalidated by the reallocation inside skb_cow_data, is recomputed from a saved offset after the copy; error propagation is correct. No stale-pointer/UAF path found.

Shared per-xfrm page_frag is fully serialized by x->lock, the lock is released on every exit (including the error goto), allocsize >= tailen so the trailer write stays within the refilled frag region, and get_page() establishes the frag's reference before the offset is advanced, preventing cross-skb page-memory reuse.

assumptions: esp->tailen/tfclen/plen are precomputed by the upstream esp6_prepare_skb() such that tailen >= tfclen + plen + 2; the analysis relies on that invariant, which holds in the upstream caller.
esp_output_fill_trailer() writes exactly tfclen + plen + 2 bytes (the upstream invariant tying it to tailen).
skb_cow_data() and skb_page_frag_refill() enforce their documented allocation guarantees.

The code is a faithful copy of the post-fix upstream net/ipv6/esp6.c esp6_output_head(), where the historical bugs (missing MAX_SKB_FRAGS check; use of the socket page_frag shared with TCP-MD5) are already remediated in this version.
limitations: Only this function was analyzed; correctness of callers (esp6_output_tail) and helpers (esp6_output_encap, esp_output_fill_trailer, skb_cow_data) was assumed from upstream semantics and could not be verified from the provided code.

An integer wrap in 'skb->data_len + tailen' was considered but rejected as unreachable with realistic skb sizes; if tailen were attacker-controlled to extreme values upstream of this function, this would need re-evaluation.
Without the full file/line metadata, evidence line numbers are approximations relative to the snippet.

verdict.summary: push_pipe() implements correct clamping (size <= i->count), ring-occupancy bounding via pipe_full() with the locally advanced iter_head, per-page length bounding via min_t(ssize_t, left, PAGE_SIZE), and publishes pipe->head only after each pipe_buffer is fully initialized. No out-of-bounds index, integer overflow, underflow, or use-after-free is reachable from the given code. Residual risk depends on caller-maintained invariants (buf->offset == 0 for the appended buffer, external locking of the pipe ring, and later iov_iter advance/revert matching the pre-extended buf->len values), which cannot be assessed from this snippet.

evidence.reason: Size is clamped to the iterator's byte count and zero-size requests are rejected before any state is touched, preventing over-requesting beyond the iterator's bounds.

The 'left <= 0' branch is taken only when size <= PAGE_SIZE - off, so buf->len += size keeps the buffer's data region within a single page. Setting len = PAGE_SIZE on the partial buffer is valid under the pipe-write invariant that such buffers have offset == 0; index access uses iter_head & p_mask, which is in-range.

The loop guard uses the locally advanced iter_head (not a stale pipe->head), so the ring occupancy (iter_head - p_tail) is checked against max_usage before each allocation. This bounds the number of allocated slots, prevents the head index from ever wrapping onto the tail, and keeps iter_head & p_mask within free slots. Allocation failure breaks cleanly without touching an uninitialized slot.

Each buffer's length is explicitly capped to PAGE_SIZE via min_t, exact byte accounting is maintained, and pipe->head is advanced only after all fields of the pipe_buffer (ops, flags, page, offset, len) are fully initialized, so readers can never observe a partially initialized buffer and no page is leaked.

assumptions: pipe->ring_size is a power of two (so p_mask = ring_size - 1 yields correct index wraparound) and pipe->max_usage <= ring_size, both standard kernel pipe invariants.
i->count does not exceed SSIZE_MAX, so the size_t-to-ssize_t assignment of left cannot truncate; kernel splice/vmsplice entry paths cap counts well below this.
For the 'if (off)' path, the partially filled buffer at iter_head has buf->offset == 0 and off is a page-relative position, so extending its len to PAGE_SIZE stays within the physical page.
Access to pipe->head, pipe->tail, and pipe->bufs is externally serialized (pipe lock/mutex held by the caller); no concurrent mutation of the ring occurs during execution.
Callers of push_pipe subsequently advance/revert the iterator and fill the provisioned pages consistently with the pre-extended buf->len values (standard iov_iter ITER_PIPE semantics).
limitations: Only this function is provided; the implementations of data_start(), pipe_full(), and the callers that establish the ITER_PIPE iterator and copy data into the provisioned pages are not shown, so caller-side invariant violations cannot be ruled out.

If a pipe buffer with buf->offset != 0 could ever be the append target in the 'if (off)' branch, buf->len = PAGE_SIZE would overclaim the page (offset + len > PAGE_SIZE), a potential out-of-bounds read; this cannot occur from buffers created by this function but depends on other code paths.

The pre-extension of buf->len before data is actually written could expose uninitialized page contents to a pipe reader if a caller fails to fill or properly revert the iterator; handling of that case lives outside this snippet and was not analyzed.
Concurrent access (lockless readers/writers racing on pipe ring fields) would be a memory-safety hazard, but synchronization is outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds write in the GLOB_TILDE user-name unescape path: the buffer 'newp' is sized 'end_name - dirname' bytes, but the unescape loop 'while (*q != "\0")' runs from 'unescape' to the NUL terminating the entire dirname string instead of stopping at 'end_name'. When dirname contains a slash after the backslash (pattern with >=2 slashes, e.g. "~\\a/AAAA.../x" with GLOB_TILDE and without GLOB_NOESCAPE), the loop copies the remainder of the path past the allocation, producing an attacker-controlled stack (alloca) or heap (malloc) buffer overflow of arbitrary length. Additionally, a NULL-pointer dereference exists at 'home_dir = strdup (p->pw_dir)' because getpwnam_r may return 0 with *result == NULL (user not found).

evidence.snippet: char *end_name = strchr (dirname, '/'); ... else unescape = memchr (dirname, '\\', end_name - dirname); ... newp = alloca_account (end_name - dirname, alloca_used); ... char *p = mempcpy (newp, dirname + 1, unescape - dirname - 1); char *q = unescape; while (*q != '\0') { if (*q == '\\') { if (q[1] == '\0') { if (filename == NULL) *p++ = '\\'; break; } ++q; } *p++ = *q++; } *p = '\0';
evidence.reason: The buffer 'newp' is allocated with exactly 'end_name - dirname' bytes, but the unescape loop is bounded only by the NUL terminating the whole dirname string, not by 'end_name'. If dirname contains a '/' located after the backslash (e.g. dirname = "~\\a/BBBB..."), the loop copies everything from 'unescape' through the rest of the path plus a NUL byte, writing past the end of the allocation. The overflow length and content are fully attacker-controlled via the glob pattern; small allocations land on the stack via alloca_account, larger ones on the heap via malloc. Example trigger: glob("~\\a/" + 'B'*100 + "/x", GLOB_TILDE, ...) overflows newp[3] by ~101 bytes.

evidence.snippet: p = NULL; err = __getlogin_r (s.data, s.length); if (err == 0) { ... err = getpwnam_r (s.data, &pwbuf, s.data + ssize, s.length - ssize, &p); } ... if (err == 0) { home_dir = strdup (p->pw_dir); malloc_home_dir = 1; }
evidence.reason: getpwnam_r may return 0 (success per POSIX) while setting the result pointer *p to NULL when the login name obtained from getlogin_r has no passwd entry (e.g. stale utmp). The code then dereferences p->pw_dir without checking p != NULL, causing a NULL-pointer dereference (denial of service).

assumptions: The code is compiled for a POSIX target (the non-WINDOWS32 paths are active); MSDOS/WINDOWS32-only blocks are excluded from the analysis.

Helper functions (next_brace_sub, glob_in_dir, prefix_array, glob_use_alloca, alloca_account, is_dir, scratch_buffer_*) behave as in glibc/gnulib: glob_use_alloca returns nonzero (stack allocation via alloca) for small requests, and next_brace_sub bounds alternatives within the brace content.

The unescape overflow is reachable only when the caller passes GLOB_TILDE or GLOB_TILDE_CHECK without GLOB_NOESCAPE and the pattern is attacker-influenced (e.g. via a scripting language or application exposing glob(3) patterns to user input).
limitations: The code was provided without line numbers; cited line numbers are approximate (estimated by counting from the start of the function).
The GLOB_ALTDIRFUNC path delegates directory access to caller-supplied function pointers; its safety depends on the caller and is out of scope for this analysis.

Helper functions (glob_in_dir, prefix_array, next_brace_sub, is_dir) are not shown, so their internal bounds could not be audited; the analysis covers only the control flow and memory operations visible in the given code.

verdict.summary: hfsplus_block_allocate() trusts on-disk HFS+ allocation-bitmap state: it never checks the return value of read_mapping_page() before kmap() (invalid-pointer dereference / kernel oops on a crafted or I/O-failing filesystem), the allocation-phase page-advance loop lacks the 'offset >= size' bounds check present in the scan loop and sets 'end' to a full page (allowing reads/writes/set_page_dirty beyond the bitmap's end when the requested run is satisfied exactly at the boundary), the 'if (n) { len = 32; }' branch overwrites the remaining request length and can mark bits beyond 'size' in the final (word-rounded) bitmap word, and 'free_blocks -= *max' is an unchecked unsigned subtraction that can underflow.

evidence.snippet:
page = read_mapping_page(mapping, offset / PAGE_CACHE_BITS, NULL);
	pptr = kmap(page);
evidence.reason: read_mapping_page() may return an error pointer (e.g., readpage failure on a corrupted allocation file); there is no IS_ERR() check before kmap()/dereference, so an attacker-supplied filesystem image can trigger an invalid-pointer dereference (kernel oops / DoS).

Unlike the scanning loop (which has 'if (offset >= size) break;'), the allocation-phase page-advance has no bounds check and unconditionally sets 'end' to a full page. When the allocation is satisfied exactly at the bitmap end (len reaches 0 with curr == end), the function reads a page past the bitmap's valid range, dereferences/kunmaps it, and marks it dirty (set_page_dirty in 'done'), i.e., access beyond the allocation file's size; kmap() of a failed read is again unchecked.

The remaining requested length is overwritten with 32. The 'last' loop then marks up to 32 free bits, ignoring both the remaining request and the 'size' boundary; because 'end' rounds size up to a word (line 25), bits at positions >= size in the final word can be marked allocated, inflating *max and corrupting bitmap/free-block accounting.

evidence.snippet:
*max = offset + (curr - pptr) * 32 + i - start;
	HFSPLUS_SB(sb).free_blocks -= *max;
evidence.reason: Unchecked unsigned subtraction of the (potentially inflated, see len=32 branch) allocated count from free_blocks; with values derived from untrusted on-disk metadata this can underflow, corrupting the filesystem's free-space state.

evidence.snippet: end = pptr + ((size + 31) & (PAGE_CACHE_BITS - 1)) / 32;
evidence.reason: 'size' is attacker-controlled on-disk data: (a) size+31 can wrap for u32 size near UINT_MAX (CWE-190), and (b) rounding up to a word boundary means the final scanned/written word includes bits beyond 'size', which combined with the len=32 branch permits marking out-of-volume blocks.

assumptions: This is Linux kernel fs/hfsplus/bitmap.c operating on untrusted on-disk HFS+ metadata (size, allocation-file contents) supplied via a mounted filesystem image.
read_mapping_page() returns an error pointer on readpage failure, per kernel semantics.
PAGE_CACHE_BITS is a power of two (multiple of 32), so the masks/divisions behave as analyzed.
limitations: Word/page-granular accesses stay within the kmap'ed page, so the primary memory-safety failure is the unchecked kmap of an error pointer, not a page-internal buffer overflow.

Exact reachability of the beyond-file page advance depends on the requested length being satisfied exactly at a page/word boundary (len reaching 0 with curr == end); the analysis shows this is reachable when size is word-aligned and trailing words are free.

The 'len = 32' over-allocation may also occur in legitimate-looking upstream code; its security impact here rests on marking bits beyond 'size' in the final rounded word and on free_blocks accounting drift/underflow.
No concrete line numbers were supplied; the reported line numbers are counted from the top of the provided snippet.

verdict.summary: The LZW prefix-chain walk decrements stackp with no lower-bound check, and the KwKwK special case can set oldcode = free_ent = maxmaxcode, an entry never written by the table-update code (guard is '< maxmaxcode', and only the first 256 entries are initialized). A crafted input can therefore drive the walk through uninitialized tab_prefix/tab_suffix values, allowing the chain to exceed the stack region (out-of-bounds write below de_stack), to cycle (hang), and to leak uninitialized memory into the decompressed output.

evidence.reason: The chain-following loop decrements stackp on every iteration with no check that stackp stays at or above the base of the stack region. Any chain longer than the region (or a cyclic chain formed from uninitialized/garbage prefixes) writes out of bounds below de_stack.

Entry definition is guarded by a strict '< maxmaxcode', so the entry at index maxmaxcode is never defined, yet the KwKwK path can make oldcode equal to free_ent == maxmaxcode, i.e., reference this undefined entry.

When code == free_ent (KwKwK), code is set to oldcode. If free_ent == maxmaxcode, the entry-add later in this iteration is skipped and 'oldcode = incode' stores the undefined maxmaxcode index; a subsequent KwKwK code then seeds the walk with the uninitialized entry tab_prefix[maxmaxcode].

Only entries 0..255 are initialized; entries 256..maxmaxcode contain uninitialized memory until defined, so any traversal that reaches an undefined index (e.g., maxmaxcode, or garbage values fetched from it) reads uninitialized memory that is then used both as loop-continuation indices and as output data.
In DEBUG builds the diagnostic reads p[-1] at an attacker-influenced buffer position, a potential out-of-bounds read below inbuf (minor, compile-time conditional).

assumptions: Table arrays (tab_prefix/tab_suffix) are sized for 2^BITS entries, so the garbage values read are in-bounds reads of uninitialized memory rather than direct OOB reads.
de_stack marks the top of a stack region whose base and exact size are defined outside the shown code; underflow means writing below that region's base.
cmp_code_int is a signed type, so the comparison (code >= 256) behaves as written for negative oldcode (-1) values.
The 'input' macro reads within inbuf because inbits is computed to keep posbits+n_bits within insize; no over-read was found on those paths.
limitations: External definitions (input macro, clear_tab_prefixof, table/stack declarations, BITS, MAXCODE) are not shown; the analysis relies on the comments and standard gzip-style definitions.
Exact line numbers are approximate because the snippet was not supplied with a numbered source file.

Reachability requires a crafted LZW stream in which the code table fills to free_ent == maxmaxcode and the code equal to free_ent is emitted twice; constructing such a stream is straightforward for an attacker since all bitstream values are attacker-controlled.
